Personal Relations Therapy: The Collected Papers of H.J.S. Guntrip edited by Jeremy Hazell. Published by Jason Aronson Inc., Northvale, New Jersey and London, 1994; 430 pages; £28.90 (hardback).

Jean Scarlett

Jean Scarlett

BAP, LCP, London

Jean Scarlett  

Jeremy Hazell's invaluable collection allows us to fill in the gaps in our knowledge of Guntrip's work and to trace the development of his thought over nearly three decades.

The book is arranged in four chronological sections: I. 1952-1958 The Fairbairn Period of ‘Broadly Oedipal’ Analysis, II. 1960-1962 The Schizoid Compromise: The Need and Fear of Regression, III. 1962-1969 The Winnicott Period: Regression and Regrowth, and IV. 1971-1978 ‘Living’: The Post-Winnicott Period.

I wish to focus particularly on one paper which seems most central and crucial. In ‘Analysis with Fairbairn and Winnicott (How Complete a Result Does PsychoAnalytic Therapy Achieve?)’, we see in a moving and significant way the connection between Guntrip's personal psychopathology and the basic principles of his theory. As he says himself: ‘The idea that we could think out a theory of the structure and functioning of the personality without its having any relation to the structure and functioning of our own personality, should be a self-evident impossibility’ (p. 368).

It was in 1949 that Guntrip decided to go into analysis with Fairbairn. He already accepted Fairbairn's rethinking of psychodynamic theory, the change from Freud's emphasis on instinct to the priority of object relations, together with his adoption of a theory of endopsychic structure containing internalised objects and potentially divided against itself. Already holding the view that psychoanalytic therapy depended not on theory but ultimately on a ‘truly understanding human relationship’ (p. 352), he felt that no intellectual disagreement would interfere with the analysis.

After three or four years Guntrip began to feel that Fairbairn, in spite of his original, logical approach, was concentrating too much in a classical way on the Oedipal level and on Guntrip's relationship with his mother as a bad object after the death of an infant brother. Guntrip felt that these phenomena were acting as a defence against a far deeper schizoid problem connected with the earliest phase of his infancy, before his brother's birth, a time when his mother completely failed to relate to him. It was left to Winnicott to make contact with the lost baby in his deep unconscious.

In Praise

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein  

Dear Editor

The Eighth Annual Lecture of the British Journal of Psychotherapy, with Peter Fonagy and Anthony Ryle presenting their ideas on psychoanalysis, cognitiveanalytic therapy, mind and self, was an intellectual feast. Thank you for making it possible. Anthony Ryle gave a clear if necessarily brief account of CAT techniques, their effects on patients, and the theoretical framework which forms their context, with an acknowledgement of indebtedness to Fairbairn, Guntrip and Winnicott. Peter Fonagy started from a consideration of the nature of mind and of self, within which context he made a number of points, the most interesting of which, from the point of view of comparison with the other speaker, concerned the depth at which he thought psychoanalysis could operate, relative to the more ego/superego-based CAT. He postulated deeply ingrained stimulus-response sequences of an object-relations kind which needed time and specifically psychoanalytic techniques, if the therapist were to reach and somehow modify them with some confidence that they would not eventually re-appear in the patient's behaviour.

Both speakers were careful to say that they were presenting unproven hypotheses which at present, in the absence of facts, could only be supported by (equally unproven) theoretical structures. Contributors from the audience in my view were less careful, and often seemed to me eager to set the two speakers by their ears.

Sitting with patients the next day, I found myself thinking at times that what was happening between them and me just at this moment would be recognised by both speakers as therapeutic, and could be described by either in terms of their own theories. This person, telling me now that ‘the kid in me is just too large, and gets hurt because other people do not like her to be there … she needs to be controlled somehow’- was she recognising something about her upbringing which had made her engage in unnecessarily difficult-to-be-with procedures at the present time, and this is therapeutic, as CAT would have it; or was she recognising, regretting, and venturing to repair something about her often difficult behaviour in the consulting-room where she tended to re-enact the many early experiences in her early life when she was out of control in the presence of an out-of-control mother, and this was the therapeutic element, as psychoanalysis would have it?

Science or Interpretive Art? Clinician, Know Thyself

Neville Singh

Neville Singh

Neville Singh  

Dear Book Reviews Editor

I am pleased to accept David Smith's invitation consequent to my letter in the Autumn 1994 issue of the Journal (VoL 11(1)). For, both his appreciative review of Adolf Grunbaum's ‘Validation in the Clinical Theory of Psychoanalysis: A Study in the Philosophy of Psychoanalysis (British Journal of Psychotherapy 10(3), 1994) and my subsequent (more anguished than intemperate) response raise vitally important, persistent questions for psychoanalysis/psychotherapy and their practitioners. Is psychoanalysis a valid scientific (perhaps more accurately, quasi-scientific) endeavour sufficiently amenable to the focused scrutiny of a philosopher of science like Grunbaum? Or is it, fundamentally, a human, i.e. interpretive-historical, science which, though intellectually disciplined, is not rigorous by virtue of its restless, ‘lawless’ subject matter (the human being/the human mind) (Abelson 1989).

To quote the psychoanalyst Alfred Margulies (1989): ‘How does one begin to approximate the inner experience of another?’. This perennial problem surely must exercise the minds and hearts of psychotherapists who during their clinical work utilise and test out tentative hypotheses about human experience and functioning to try and answer that question, and revise or modulate or indeed discard their interventions (interpretations) in light of their patients’ responses or lack of response.

Clinical Commentary XVII

[The material was sent ‘blind’ to three clinicians who were asked to comment on the session and on how their way of thinking about the patient would inform their way of working with him. - MB]

The Therapist Writes

John - 10 Years of Age

This session was taken from the middle of John's third term of three times a week psychotherapy. John lives with his parents and is the eldest of three children; they are a middle-class family. There was a previous miscarriage before John's birth. The second child, Mark, was born when John was 18 months old and the third child was born a couple of years later. Mark suffered a life-threatening illness, and the couple managed by dividing their care. Mother looked after Mark whilst John was looked after by his father. John began suffering from severe epilepsy at 18 months, but he has been stable for many years and has not been on medication for some time. John was eventually referred because of his odd and unmanageable behaviour which perplexed both his family and the staff at his special school. John habitually lived in a world of his own leaving him developmentally delayed in all spheres.

The following is a Monday session. There had been some uncertainty about transport, and we had spoken about it in the previous session.

John's dad acknowledged my arrival by looking at John, then up to the heavens in ‘mock’ despair. Meanwhile John was grinning widely, perhaps to himself. When he saw me he literally dropped what he was doing and eagerly joined me. He half spoke to me, mumbling in an excited way whilst flicking his hands ritualistically. Once in the room he calmed and opened his box taking out his telephone. ‘Now, boys and girls, I'm Miss Smith.’ I knew this to be the name of his teacher. He continued in this way and I spoke to him about how it seemed that right now John had gone. I talked then about how hard it was to be John at school, then John at the clinic, to be one place, then the other. John then seemed to leave his Miss Smith character and told me how he had to go straight back to school because his dad had to take the car back to the garage. I said that John had been worried not knowing whether he would be able to make it today. He looked at me with surprise and asked me how I knew this. I said that it seemed hard to remember how he had told me about the car difficulty last week.

British Journal of Medical Psychology67, 305-317, 1994

The Role of Insight in Exploratory Psychodynamic Psychotherapy

Per Hoglend, Vibeke Engelstad, Oystein Sorbye, Oscar Heyerdahl and Svein Amlo

Psychoanalytic theory holds that dynamic insight is used for self-observation and self-analysis during and after explorative therapy. Such self-analysis is held to lead to stable dynamic change. Within a sample of 43 moderately disturbed out-patients, pre-treatment level of insight was associated with treatment length, with not being an early or late dropout, and with receiving additional psychotherapy during a four-year follow-up period. Pre-treatment level of insight turned out to be not directly correlated with outcome two and four years after therapy. However, level of insight was significantly correlated with outcome in interaction with treatment length. Gain of insight measured at two-year follow-up was the strongest predictor of overall dynamic change four years after therapy, compared with all the other outcome assessments made at two-year follow-up.



Psychotherapy Research4(2), 121-135, 1994

Alliance and Technique for Predicting Outcome in Short- and Long-Term Analytic Psychotherapy

Louise Gaston, William E. Piper, Elie G. Debbane, Jean-Pierre Bienvenu and Jacques Garant

A previous clinical trial provided the opportunity to examine the roles and interaction of alliance and technique in both short- and long-term analytic psychotherapy. Two separate teams of trained clinical judges rated either alliance on the CALPAS or therapist interventions on the ITS. Outcome included symptomatology and interpersonal problems. In short-term therapy, working and therapeutic alliance ratings contributed significantly to the reduction of symptomatology only. In longterm therapy, working alliance ratings contributed significantly to the reduction of interpersonal problems, and the interaction of working alliance ratings with supportive or exploratory intervention rating was found to account for significant amounts of the variance of both symptomatology and interpersonal problems at termination. These findings should be considered with caution, given the restricted sample sizes.

Laurie Wright

Laurie Wright

Laurie Wright  

Nini Herman's new book, Letters to the Living and the Dead, has left me in a dilemma as to how to approach it for review. This is an extraordinarily candid and personal book - and on the one hand I am full of admiration for Dr Herman's courage to be so forthright and self-analytical. On the other hand, I find myself questioning whether it is really appropriate that a practising clinician should be publishing such self-revealing material.

Briefly, the book consists of ten chapters: an introduction outlining the premise and motivation behind the writing of this book, which is followed by nine ‘letters’ addressed to individuals who have been significant figures in the author's life. The recipients include members of her own family: a male relation, her grandmother, and her parents, and three friends: Bessie Head, Adele Wiseman, and Michael Peto, all of whom are dead. The living recipients are her husband, the painter Josef Herman, and the writer Toni Morrison.

Ring of Fire: Primitive Affects and Object Relations in Group Psychotherapy edited by Victor L. Schermer and Malcolm Pines. Published by Routledge, London, 1994; 316 pages; £16.99 (paperback).

Chris Evans

Chris Evans

London

Chris Evans  

This book aims to bring together ‘new and original contributions to an understanding of primitive object relations and of those highly charged emotional states which present the maximum challenge to the group psychotherapist: the “Ring of Fire” (p. 2). Seven of the 11 authors are from the States, three from Britain, and Resnik is the only contributor from outside that Anglophone alliance (based in France, writing about work he did as a visiting analyst in Italy).

Resnik's chapter is on ‘Glacial times in psychotic regression’ and is the crowning glory of a good book. Resnik describes a group for psychotic inpatients watched from behind a one-way screen by staff members. The material crackles with the eponymous ‘fire’ of psychotic delusions and hallucinations but also shows the glacial retreats which defend against psychotic anxieties. A patient comments, pointing to an old scar on a finger, ‘This is the scar from an old wound. Before awakening an old wound, you doctors ought to know the coagulation time of the patient’. In their foreword to the chapter Schermer and Pines suggest that readers may find Resnik's use of depth interpretation in acute psychosis controversial. I did not. What I found controversial was that Resnik makes little of the possible relation between his approach and the completed suicide of a young female member of the group. His quoting the other patient on possible psychic exsanguination shows his sensitivity, and mention of the observing group providing intermittent practical containment of the patients suggests that he and the watchers were alive to the dangers. I suspect that one suicide in the lifetime of this group is not statistically improbable in comparison with more conventional treatment programmes but I would have liked Resnik to have said more about the group's, and his own, processing of the death.

258

Ignatius of Loyola: The Psychology of a Saint by W. W. Meissner. Published by Yale University Press, 1994; 500 pages; £11.50.

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

London

Josephine Klein  

Meissner's Ignatius may be of particular interest to those of us who ponder about formulations of mystical religious experiences which might be compatible with our understanding of psychodynamic processes. His previous work suggests that Meissner, who is both a Jesuit and a (North American) psychoanalyst, may long have been reflecting on these issues.

If we share this concern, we might do best to start with the book's final chapter, ‘The spiritual ascent’, which turns on Meissner's understanding of Winnicott's concept of illusion. This, he points out, is very different from Freud's. For Freud, mystical experiences were regressions to states of infantile dependence; Winnicott conceived of transitional experiences and potential spaces. The hallucinated breast of Winnicott's theory can coincide with a breast presented by the mother at the very moment at which the infant desires and imagines it. At that moment infant and breast are at one both subjectively and objectively. Meissner here considers mystical religious experience as an experience in potential space, the religious object as an object to be met there. An interesting possibility.

The book is best taken as a commentary on this idea. Hence, after ‘The spiritual ascent’, I recommend Chapters 16, 17 and 19, ‘The mystic’, ‘The ascetic’ and ‘Mysticism’, before starting more conventionally at Chapter one. Readers particularly interested in the problems of epistemology and phenomenology may likewise prefer to pick and choose to start with. The introductory section on historiography, psychohistory and psychobiography was very instructive.

265

Nathan Field

Nathan Field

London

Nathan Field  

The prologue to Dr Rosen's book describes how, while still a medical student, he came near to committing suicide provoked by his wife's rejection. In the ensuing despair he consulted a psychiatrist-friend who said: ‘You are not a failure. You failed

272

at marriage’. In the years that followed Rosen became a psychiatrist specializing in depression, then a Jungian analyst, and currently holds the unique position of Professor of Analytical Psychology at Texas A & M University.

His personal trauma effectively contains the essence of his work: the conversion of suicide into what he terms ‘egocide’. By this he means the renunciation of a specific ego ideal - successful husband, lover, mother, businessman, entertainer etc. - which formerly gave life its meaning. To work through the loss of such a narcissistic investment means discovering, at the same time, one's true self: this is his notion of transformation.

Rosen cites Elvis Presley as an example of someone who could not accept loss of a particular status, his status as the ‘King’ of pop. In spite of being a multi-millionaire and national icon, he progressively drank and drugged himself to death. By contrast, Rosen recalls various individuals - Abraham Lincoln, John Stuart Mill, William James - who became suicidally depressed in their early years but battled through to become ‘weller than well’ and men of outstanding achievement. Jung himself is a well-known example, his most creative work developing after the depths of the severe mental illness which followed his break with Freud. Nor is the transformation confined to exceptional individuals. While still a medical student Rosen chose, as a research project, to interview the very few individuals who had survived an attempt at suicide by jumping off the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco.

The ten survivors gave various reasons for jumping, but there was a common core feeling of aloneness, alienation, depression, rejection, worthlessness, and hopelessness. Although the ten had widely divergent views of religion before attempting suicide, they all admitted to feelings of spiritual transcendence after they had leaped. (p. xxiii)

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Spiritual Connection: A Dilemma for Psychotherapists?

Jill Hopkins

Jill Hopkins

Badgers Hay
Kingston St Mary
Taunton TA2 8HU

Jill Hopkins  

There can be few psychotherapists unaware of the greater interest in religion and the spiritual life these days. Never before have so many books on the subject been published and actually read. The demand for retreats, pastoral counsellors and workshops on spirituality has grown steadily over the last decade. There seems to be a real hunger for more knowledge and understanding of these issues, a need which institutionalised religion, in the East or West, is meeting only to a limited extent. For many, it is a pilgrimage they continue mostly on their own.

Since so many people are asking questions about the meaning of life and their personal response, it is quite likely that a significant proportion of them will also seek some form of counselling or psychotherapy. So how do their spiritual concerns affect their choices of psychotherapists, the developments and endings of their therapies? And how do the psychotherapists respond to such patients? Is there a respect for spirituality on a par with sex and gender, race and culture, physical health and intellectual or artistic attainments?

It seems that the taboo on the religious and spiritual, set up by psychoanalysis, is beginning to shift. Papers on these issues are being published in the most reputable journals and for some time now Karnac has stocked books on the subject. But it is still an area filled with the greatest anxiety, prejudice and ignorance for many psychotherapists and psychoanalysts. The old arguments about illusions, psychosis, immaturity, deviancy, obsessional preoccupations, wish-fulfilments, splitting and childish projections do not hold the truth when set alongside a healthy, well-informed life of faith and practice. The psychoanalytic world in general has not caught up with the cutting-edge of modern spirituality in any of the world religions. Of course, there are exceptions among the psychoanalytically trained and it is thanks to them that this taboo is beginning to lift. Jungians have always respected the spiritual dimension though they have not always gone as far as the cutting edge, preferring the mystery of traditional forms rather than more recent approaches to belief, prayer and worship. Obviously each one of us reflects our particular psychopathological state in the way we respond to any of this.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

In everyday life, those instantaneous, very first impressions can be so important that they, quite unfairly, form the basis of all future judgements of the other person and dictate the nature of the relationship. Crucial, too, for the course of a relationship are expectations of the other, and there is a large literature in psychological studies that shows the role played by expectations in shaping and predicting relationships. The particular kind of expectation that we find in psychotherapy, conceptualised as the transference, is believed to be present even before the first meeting. The concentration of energic forces focused on to the first psychotherapy session, a highly-charged mixture of excitement, fear, hope, despair, need, desire and defence, can create the circumstances for seminal communications, from the subtle to the dramatic. Interestingly, in an audiotaped study of a five-year, five-times-a-week analysis (by Hartvig Dahl in the USA (personal communication, 1990)), a content analysis revealed that all the themes and conflicts that were important to the analysis were present in the very first session. Two papers in this issue look at ‘beginnings’: Gail Yariv writes of being receptive to the transference-countertransference impact in the first moments as a valuable point of reference for understanding ‘core object relations’, and Charles Rycroft discusses the procedure for conducting a patient into treatment, ‘classical’ and revised. I hope that readers will be moved to contribute more thoughts on this topic.

Pychoanalytic psychotherapy with couples is on the move. The Tavistock Marital Studies Institute is initiating a well-designed research project in conjunction with Professor Peter Hobson's Developmental Psychopathology Research Unit at the Tavistock Centre in order to provide experimental data for analytic work with couples. In this issue Warren Coleman from the TMSI writes from a Jungian perspective about gender confusions and insecurities in marital psychotherapy.

Shirley Hover

Child Psychotherapist, formerly Tavistock Clinic, London

Shirley Hover  

This is a book which crosses boundaries and opens the way for creative surges towards more integrative therapeutic interventions in the manifold experiences of suffering in both body and mind. The contributors are multidisciplinary and their psychoanalytic approaches derive from differing theoretical backgrounds. They work in diverse settings, with children, adolescents and adults suffering from a broad range of conditions. Yet the book is not just a collection of disparate papers. It has a cohesion, as all the writers are engaged in a thrust towards innovative work in applying psychoanalytic thinking to the health care of those whose dysfunctions are both physical and mental.

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

Lincoln Centre, London

Robert Tollemache  

Fairbairn was the first to challenge head on Freud's theory of libidinal drives and his structural theory of the personality while remaining securely within the psychoanalytic fold. His alternative formulations are borne out by the researches of Bowlby, Ainsworth and other attachment theorists, as well as the researches of Stem, Brazelton, Cramer and others who research the developing relationship between mothers and babies. This may be why there seems to be a rediscovery of Fairbairn at present; this book is both a product of and a contribution to this renewal of interest. It is predominantly by North American writers and displays a trend among them to seek to reconcile and assimilate varying schools of thought, e.g. Fairbairn's ideas and those of Ego psychologists or Kohutian Self-psychologists. This might suggest that the book is primarily aimed at the American market. However there are also contributions by a number of British analysts and psychotherapists.

It is a big work, consisting of 17 essays, an epilogue and three appendices. It is complex, and, as well as covering every aspect of Fairbairn's work, opposing points of view are offered. As the editors say, the book is best considered a complement to Sutherland's Fairbairn's Journey into the Interior, and Fairbairn's own Psychoanalytic Studies of the Personality, and is a serious study aid. After some introductory papers, it is divided into a theoretical and a clinical section, followed by papers on how Fairbairn's work relates to ideas about the Self. Perhaps the overriding experience is of the strength and fertility of Fairbairn's formulations, which have provoked so many diverse, fruitful strands of thought.

There is a good deal of repetition with so many writers dealing with the same subject, but this has the advantage of helping one understand Fairbairn's work from a number of points of view. The concept of ‘Object’ in Fairbairn's and Klein's theories, by Mitchell, is particularly helpful, especially in tracing the evolution of Klein's ideas of the Object and how they compare with Fairbairn's stricter and more constant but less fertile view. Indeed, throughout the book, the close links between them, and the interrelating development of their ideas, is explained.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Head of Psychology and Psychotherapy Services, Lister Hospital, Stevenage

Phil Mollon  

At a recent psychoanalytic congress between British Independents and US self-psychologists, I asked a number of those who had known Kohut what he had been like as a teacher. Typical replies were: ‘a genius’, ‘outstanding’, ‘brilliant’ - and this from some who disagreed with aspects of his work. Yet few in Britain seem to have much understanding of what a wonderful thing is self-psychology, how it illuminates many common clinical problems and therapeutic impasses and leads the therapist into an easier and gentler way of working.

These two books provide an excellent overview of contemporary self-psychology, which seems to have evolved into two schools since Kohut's death in 1982 - the ‘classical’ school based in Chicago where many of the practitioners trained directly with Kohut, and the post-Kohutian theorists of intersubjectivity based in Los Angeles, where Stolorow is a leading figure. Of the two books, Mahler and Kohut stays closer to the work of these two theorists and includes some very competent comparisons of their respective views of psychological development and the implications of these for psychoanalytic treatment. The eight chapters were originally papers presented at the Twenty-fifth Margaret Mahler Symposium on Child Development in 1993. A particularly valuable chapter is Ernest Wolf's on ‘Selfobject Experiences: Development, Psychopathology, Treatment’.

The three major elements of this fascinating correspondence are: the way in which the relationship between the two men evolves, as Ferenczi moves from awestruck young stranger to valued colleague and friend, and from disciple to bold innovator; the account it gives of the first great schism in psychoanalysis, as first Adler and then Jung break with Freud; and the light it throws on Ferenczi's preoccupation with boundaries.

Commentary by a Post-Kleinian Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Eric Rhode

Eric Rhode

28 Holland Park
London W11 3TA

Eric Rhode  

We learn no facts from the session about John's mother. But as an ontological presence, as a condensed state of being that you could cut with a knife, she is the session: she fills space and time. It is John and his therapist (by way of John's projections) who behave as though they thought themselves to be non-existent. In this oppressive atmosphere of anti-imagination, both of them might be a kind of stuff in the mother's mind.

As a hypothesis, I would suggest that the pressure of at least two shocks that she could not tolerate has impelled John's mother to mould John into a figment of a grief she could not stand. The first shock is of the miscarriage: a loss perhaps conceived of as a gap, the gap being translated into John as the gap-ghost. The second shock is Mark's birth when John is aged 18 months. Round about this time, Mark has a ‘lifethreatening illness’ and John begins to suffer from severe epilepsy. Again as a hypothesis, I wonder whether John's mother went into another blankness when faced by Mark's life-threatening disease. I am put in mind of the theory that a trauma occurs when someone at least twice fails to register an emotional shock. John might be the configuration of a trauma: it is as though traumas were print-outs on the plasticine of the body.

John, the ghostly simulacrum of a miscarriage, is now transformed into a somatic agitation. His body does not act as though it has been mentally born into a community of shared experience. It is tortured by fits, as though the idea of embodiment had been turned inside out: it talks in minus speak.

Medication controls the epilepsy but (so far as we can see) it does not modify John's ontological state of being possessed.

612

A View from the Receiving End

Kirsty Hall

Kirsty Hall

134 Dukes Avenue, Muswell Hill, London N10 2QB

Kirsty Hall  

“What is truth?” said jesting Pilate and would not stay for an answer.' This is the opening line of an essay by Bacon, who is unable to supply anything more than a few well-chosen aphorisms on a notoriously knotty subject. I wonder if people really bother to ask the same fundamental question about education, and, in particular, about psychoanalytic education. What is it, what does it consist in? The articles by Jeremy Holmes, Martin Stanton and Jane Kitto in the Winter 1993 and Autumn 1994 numbers of this Journal suggest that the psychoanalytic world is trying to avoid asking it at all costs. One person who at least attempts to explain the meaning of the term is Raymond Williams (1976) in his delightful book Keywords - A Vocabulary of Culture and Society.

The entry for educated starts as follows:

To educate was originally to rear or bring up children, from educare (Latin) - to rear or foster (rather than from educere - lead forth, develop, of which educare is an intensive form) … The wide sense has never quite been lost but it has been specialized to organized teaching and instruction since the early Seventeenth Century and predominantly so since the late Eighteenth Century. (Williams 1976, pp. 111-2)

Since the central thesis of psychoanalysis is indeed that the child is the father of the man (perhaps more politically and psychoanalytically correctly, the child is the parents of the person) then it could be said that we are all engaged in a process of analysing education in its original and, I think, its most appealing sense.

So, how is this reflected in the realities of a psychoanalytic education? In practical terms education is subsumed to and paradoxically both mysteriously and prosaically becomes the process of being taught, of being trained, of learning, or the experience of being a student. I have been a trainee psychotherapist with the Arbours, or more elegantly, a psychotherapist in training. I hope that I remain the latter whilst, if I am honest, I am relieved that I no longer have to bear with the former since I qualified in 1994. I still qualify for the label ‘student’, however, since I am in the second year of a part-time M.A. in Psychoanalysis at Middlesex University.

Psychoanalysis in Transition: A Personal View by Merton M. Gill. Published by The Analytic Press, New Jersey, 1994; 200 pages; $29.95.

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

London

Susan Budd  

American psychoanalysts see classical psychoanalysis as being challenged from two slightly different positions; the first being what Merton Gill calls the relational perspective, which is roughly equivalent to the British object relations school, and the second being self-psychology. In this overview of changes and developments in psychoanalytic theory, he tries to relate the clinical aspects of these theories to their wider philosophical and epistemological bases, i.e. the shift between natural science and hermeneutics, and positivism to constructivism. (I think we would probably say subjectivism.) Gill has been involved in the theoretical move away from classical theory to a more relational view of transference, but in this book he tries to summarize the strengths and weaknesses of each position as impartially as he can. One problem for the British reader is that he assumes quite a high level of familiarity with the details of the arguments as presented in the American literature. The book contains virtually no clinical material; many British psychotherapists, being empirically minded, will probably reject it immediately on that account. But, although it is by no means an easy read, it does set out in a systematic way the various alternative assumptions that must underlie all our clinical statements, whether we are aware of them or not, and along the way he makes many interesting, sensible, even creative, comments and connections between different aspects of psychoanalytical therapy.

He starts out by discussing the various theories about the role of internal and external reality. The central tenet of psychoanalytic theory is that internal fantasy is the expression of universal innate drives, but throughout its history there has been debate as to what extent reality external to the subject needs to be taken account of in explaining his or her state of mind. The two later positions tend to stress the interrelations between subject and subjectively viewed object - or selfobject - and, more importantly, unlike classical theory, stress deficit as well as conflict. As throughout the book, he considers that the difference between the theories is not either/or, but lies in a careful consideration of relative emphases.

Meeting Freud's Family by Paul Roazen. Published by University of Massachusetts Press, Amherst, MA, 1993; 220 pages; £24.00.

David Smith

David Smith

London

David Smith  

Meeting Freud's Family is Paul Roazen's most recent contribution to the historiography of psychoanalysis. The book describes Roazen's interviews with members of Freud's family, including three of his children (Anna, Mathilda and Oliver), a daughter-in-law (Esti) and a sister-in-law (Henny). The book is also peppered with information from interviews with members of Freud's metaphorical family, the psychoanalytic movement. Material from the interviews is interspersed with personal impressions of the interviewees and their circumstances and brief accounts of important episodes in the history of psychoanalysis.

Roazen's style is lucid and relaxed. He is also candid in a way which would be impossible for someone within the psychoanalytic community. Some readers may find Roazen's irreverence offensive. For instance, he describes the Hampstead Clinic as having ‘a musty atmosphere of old-fashioned nursery school teachers talking with barely suppressed prurience about the implications of “infantile sexuality“’ (p. 86). A good deal of the book is devoted to Anna Freud who emerges as a censorious autocrat. I found Roazen's exposition refreshing and at times amusing though ultimately sad. The irrationality, paranoia and general interpersonal chaos within the psychoanalytic world create a rather pathetic impression when considered in the light of its spiritual pretensions.

Meeting Freud's Family adds to our understanding of the history of psychoanalysis and Sigmund Freud by drawing on the memories of those few people still alive in the 1960s who knew Freud intimately. There are also lots of good photographs, including an incredibly moving one of a sad, tired Freud taken just before his death. The book will be of considerable interest to anyone interested in the history of psychoanalysis. I had difficulty putting it down and regretted reaching the final page.

David Smith

NHS Psychotherapy

Alasdair MacDonald

Alasdair MacDonald

Alasdair MacDonald  

Dear Editor

You were kind enough to publish my paper ‘Training and outcome in supervised individual psychotherapy’ in 1992 (British Journal of Psychotherapy 8(3):237-46). We have continued to collect information on cases seen since then. However, changed circumstances in the new NHS will prevent further study of these cases. Your readers may be interested in a brief summary of recent cases.

A total of 87 referrals were made, with two consultant psychiatrists responsible for almost half of them. 9 patients had hyperventilation disorder, 17 were referred for solution-focused brief therapy or other forms of psychotherapy, 30 refused psychotherapy or were unsuitable and 31 were referred for treatment. Follow-up data are available for 23 treated cases but information comes only from contacts with the mental health services (unlike the previous study where all regional agencies and general practitioners were contacted).

The mean age of the sample was 34.13 years [SD 9.45, range 19-48 years]. 6 were male and 17 female. 8 patients presented with anxiety and 6 with depression and there were 2 who complained of both. 5 patients reported major relationship problems complicated by anxiety or depression. 1 patient had post-traumatic stress disorder and 1 was anxious and abused alcohol. Patients attended for a mean of 39.17 sessions [SD 20.66; range 10-79 sessions]. The follow-up period ranged from 1 month to 69 months after finishing treatment [mean 34.17; SD 20.37].

17 patients [74%] have had no further contact with mental health services. 2 patients [8.7%] had much reduced contact, 1 patient [4.4%] had as much contact as formerly and 3 patients [13%] had much increased contact with mental health services. Therapists predicting outcome at discharge were correct in only 10 of the 23 cases.

These results on a limited follow-up can be compared with our previous detailed analysis of 25 cases in which 17 [68%] had no further contact with any other agency and less contact with their GPs while 4 patients [16%] were clearly worse and required extensive further contact with various agencies. There is, therefore, continued support for the conclusion that individual psychodynamic psychotherapy improves mental health and social function in 68-74% of patients, as shown by a reduction in use of specialist services.

From Dependency to Autonomy: Studies in Organisation and Change by Eric Miller. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1994; 330 pages; £16.95.

Robin Piper

Robin Piper

London

Robin Piper  

Eric Miller is an author who has an important place as a guide to our understanding of organizations and their behaviour and whose contributions have given him a quite unique position and status at the epicentre of a new discipline. Any book by him has to be taken seriously for the new ideas it can offer which extend our knowledge of the functioning of complex groups.

In the preface to this, his latest publication, Miller says, ‘action research is clinical research’, and the book, much of the material for which has developed out of his studies at the Tavistock Institute for Human Relations, is very much about putting this concept into practice.

Miller suggests an important distinction between the role of the internal and external consultant. The latter allows for independence and, in his view, greater autonomy and integrity. This paradigm runs like a golden thread throughout the book and in part accounts for the title From Dependency to Autonomy. In the first chapter, ‘Values and concepts’, Miller draws on the thinking of Klein, Bion, Lewin, Rice, Lawrence and others to illustrate his intellectual ground plan. Part 2, ‘People preceding processing institutions’, considers three studies of people. Some of the information published in this chapter has been printed earlier and has made fascinating re-reading in this new publication.

The work referred to in Part 3, ‘Analysis and diagnosis’, I found particularly enjoyable, the description of the work of the Church of England especially as I was in a similar situation for 10 years, running a clergy support group, and can therefore absolutely agree with Miller's statement that ‘many curates fear they are in difficult and isolated positions in their parishes and welcome the opportunity to compare roles with others’ (p. 112). This sense of isolation, I am sure, can also be well recognized by psychotherapists in private practice.

In Part 4, ‘Process of development and change’, Miller addresses a fundamental premise: if you wish systems to change from a dependency culture to one of autonomy, ‘the nature of the relationship is a critical factor in the process of the development of change’ (p. 174). In this chapter he argues that the participation of the client population is an important element in the approach of the development agency. One could argue that this is the touchstone from which psychotherapy should similarly operate.

Reader's Resistance or Author's Communication Failure?

Tirril Harris

Tirril Harris

11 Bedford Square, London WC 1B 3RA

Tirril Harris  

This is a response to Langs and Badalamenti's response on the question of a formal science for psychoanalysis. Earlier in the year I sent a longer draft of it directly to Dr Langs, who replied personally to me with what seemed like an olive branch. He pointed out that it was not only he, but many other readers, who had found the tone of my original piece (Harris 1994) pretty hostile. This seemed to me to justify my going into print once again, partly in apology, and partly in an attempt to convey more clearly what I consider a balanced position on this topic. In my original commentary I ended by likening work trying to operationalize the promise of psychoanalysis as a science to the construction of tunnels under the ocean, and expressed the hope that workers using Langs and Badalamenti's methods would soon join tunnels with other research workers, approaching as it were from another direction. Here I cited work studying attachment and meaning, the potential combination of which has recently caused optimism that ‘the empirical study of human psychology need no longer be seen as opposed to hermeneutics’ (Ryle 1995). It is my continued hope that we and our colleagues will ultimately achieve this kind of conjuncture of perspectives, and I feel that in the interim there is considerable value in monitoring the clarity of each other's communications.

It seems I am hoist by my own petard. The very point I was raising against Langs and Badalamenti's (1994a) paper about a formal science for psychoanalysis - namely that they have not succeeded in clearly communicating their meaning - must also apply to my comments on their paper, judging by the way they have reacted. So I am prompted to try the patience of the Journal's readership one last time in an effort to convey what I consider an important message. As often happens with communication failures, both in sessions and in everyday life, they have reacted in an all-or-none way: because I have raised some critical points they have not been able to hear how much I am on their side. They have felt totally ‘dismissed’ (Langs & Badalamenti (1994b), p. 305) instead of seeing that my criticisms were not about what they aim to do but about whether the means they are using appear to be capable of achieving these aims. In retrospect I attribute their reaction less to resistance on their part and more to a failure on my part to communicate clearly this basic alliance. My fundamental agreement with the authors that psychoanalytic therapists must try to move forward in a framework of scientific methodology (Harris 1994, p. 110) clearly got lost for them in the plethora of my metaphors about food and sand tunnels.

[[RunningHead]]

The Greenwich Consortium of Psychotherapists

The Greenwich Consortium of Psychotherapists (GCP) is a group of psychoanalytic psychotherapists and analysts working within the Greenwich area of south-east London. The 10 council members come from a variety of backgrounds and trainings; all are UKCP members and some also belong to the BCP. Future members and associates will be welcomed from the wide membership base that forms the Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and Analytical Psychology sections of the UKCP, and the BCP.

GCP members work in private practice with adults, couples and children. Some also work within the health and education services as therapists; many members also teach aspects of psychoanalysis, psychotherapy and psychology at postgraduate level in a number of universities and psychotherapy training organizations.

Members of the GCP share a keen awareness of the lack of high-quality psychoanalytic psychotherapy services for clients, trained practitioners and other professionals in south-east London. With the concentration of training organizations in north London, the majority of psychotherapists and analysts practise north of the Thames and thus most postgraduate opportunities for supervision, research, conferences and courses cluster in these areas. Not only is this inconvenient for travelling, it also takes practitioners away from their local community with its specific needs.

The GCP is aware of the need for a locally based organization that can respond to the demands of allied professions, by offering psychoanalytic psychotherapy perspectives and expertise from a position within the same community as the professionals themselves. This fosters a practical understanding of psychoanalytic psychotherapy while helping to integrate different ways of working. By offering courses and training within the community, the Greenwich Consortium of Psychotherapists hopes to encourage those working locally to attend training and workshops that would seem more remote, in both senses, if held outside the area.

The immediate plans of the Consortium include the provision of training, workshops and conferences at the postgraduate level designed to meet the needs of professionals within the framework of social services, education, NHS and the judicial system.

Patients as Victims: Sexual Abuse in Psychotherapy and Counselling edited by Derek Jehu. Published by John Wiley and Sons, 1994; 214 pages; £17.95 (paperback).

David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

This book represents one of the growing attempts to deal with the problem of sexual relationships developing between therapists and their clients. It takes the view, rightly in my opinion, that this amounts to sexual abuse even if the client consents or initiates. Ultimate responsibility always rests with the therapist.

The book is an easy read, quite accessible, and attempts to produce some solid data about the nature and extent of sexual abuse in the therapy business. For example, some statistics reveal that something under 10% of therapists have sexual contact with their clients and that this is right across the board, since the kind of training the therapist has received does not affect this figure. Another figure that makes an impact is that 80% of clients who had sexual contact with their therapists report they were psychologically harmed by the experience. The book also attempts to disentangle the issues around sexual relationships that develop during the therapy and those that start after the therapy has finished. Again, the view is taken that it remains abuse even after the therapy has been terminated. Many readers will probably agree with this.

The book attempts, to explore systematically various aspects of the problem with sections on ethics, epidemiology, characteristics of abusive therapists and their victims. It finishes with ideas on regulation and prevention. Though there were items of interest in each section the shortcomings were also apparent.

The book is written by, and may well appeal most to, cognitive-behavioural psychologists. Much of the analysis and discussion lacks the depth and richness that psychodynamic readers might be more at home with. Most of the research is statistical with what seems to my mind an over-valuation of questionnaires. Chapter 4 on the epidemiology in the UK is based entirely on a survey of clinical psychologists in this country. It is fine as far as it goes, but the reader is left wondering about what such a survey would reflect: will all the abusing therapists respond to a questionnaire; of those that respond how is it possible to know if they are fabricating or being honest about committing, or the extent of, the abuse?

Abstracts from other Journals

Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy9(2), 121-131, 1995

Biological and Psychic Domains: Clinical and Institutional Aspects Marco Chiesa

This paper attempts to tackle some of the issues present in the relationship between the theories of a psychology of mind and the theories of neuroscience. The ancient and seemingly-unsolvable mind-body problem may find a more fertile ground for debate through pragmatic clinical presentation than pure metaphysical and philosophical discussions. Some aspects from the psychoanalysis of a subject suffering from a rare genetic abnormality, and a brief vignette from the life of a psychiatric institution, are presented and discussed, to exemplify some of the complexities present at the interface between the psychic and biological domains.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy9(2), 107-120, 1995

Is the Brain More Real than the Mind? Mark Solms

This paper reflects on the place of psychoanalytical thinking in a scientific context in which mental illness is increasingly being reduced to physiological and chemical factors. A small series of neurological patients with severe emotional disturbances is presented, in order to demonstrate that emotional symptoms can be neither described nor explained in physical terms. Even in cases where an organic aetiology is indisputable, physiological factors can only be invoked to explain somatic symptoms and the physiological correlates of mental symptoms. The mental symptoms themselves can only be understood psychologically.



International Journal of Psycho Analysis76, 315, 1995

The Role of the Father in a Pre-Suicide State Donald Campbell

In the self-examination that followed a patient's suicide attempt, the author was worried by three features which he had observed in an earlier suicide attempt by another patient: (1) the father had not featured in the analysis as much as would have been expected, (2) the suicide attempt occurred during a period when the time and place boundaries of the analytic setting were in jeopardy, e.g. the patient was absent from sessions; and (3) this coincided with the author having temporarily underestimated the suicidal risk. These three features were illuminated by a transference to a father who did not claim his child for himself and offered an alternative to fusion with a dangerous mother. Although the patient's suicide fantasies were based on a pathological bond with his mother, during the pre-suicide state the internalized father who had failed to protect his son from mother was evoked in the countertransference to function as a sanction for the suicidal act.

From Freud's Consulting Room: The Unconscious in a Scientific Age by Judith M. Hughes. Published by Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA, 1994; 235 pages; £22. 25.

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

London

Robert Tollemache  

I have really enjoyed this short and intriguing book. Ms Hughes, who seems to be primarily an academic rather than a practitioner, argues that Freud was forced into gradually developing his views of the mind-body relationship as he attempted to formulate his patients' difficulties, and she traces these developments through the case studies.

The case studies are summarized only but it is refreshing to have them all brought together in one place. The way Freud's work grew is outlined boldly and confidently and themes are linked together from case to case. Ms Hughes shows great depth of knowledge through her use not only of the case histories but also of the surrounding material, including letters, all that has been published about the various patients and, particularly interesting, Freud's self analysis.

[[RunningHead]]

Reminiscences of a Survivor: Psychoanalysis 1937-1993

Charles Rycroft

Charles Rycroft

2 Modbury Gardens, London NW5 3QE

Charles Rycroft  

I must confess that one of the reasons why I accepted the invitation to speak to you this evening is that I have always been much attached to Regent's Park, which I have known well, perhaps even intimately, since October 1937, which was when I started medicine at University College in Gower Street and started my training analysis with Ella Sharpe in Kent Terrace. As my analytical session began at 5.30 p.m., it was possible and convenient to walk daily, five times a week, across Regent's Park from Gower Street to Kent Terrace.

The previous year, two Cambridge friends and I had applied for training at the Institute of Psychoanalysis and I had eventually been accepted, after interviews with Ernest Jones, Glover and Rickman, on condition that I did medicine. This condition was insisted upon, I now think, for two reasons: to ensure that I could not start practising analysis until I was over 30, and to test out whether I was really serious about becoming an analyst. Ernest Jones suspected me of being a dilettante, and did indeed call me one during one of my interviews with him.

I should explain that in the 1930s Freudian psychoanalysis was regarded as deeply subversive. In progressive, advanced circles, Marx and Freud were regarded as the archenemies of capitalist society and middle-class morality, and to announce that one intended to become an analyst was indeed a gesture calculated pour épater les bourgeois. In fact, of course, British psychoanalysis in the 1930s was more an offshoot of Bloomsbury than a wing of any revolutionary movement, but I did not realise that at the time, despite the fact that it was Karin Stephen, a sister-in-law of Virginia Woolf, who pushed, prodded and dared me to apply for training.

Of the years spent in analysis with Ella Sharpe I can remember more about Regent's Park than I can about my sessions in Kent Terrace. I do remember that Ella Sharpe thought highly of me, which was flattering but embarrassing, and also that she worried about me, which was an alarming and novel experience for me. What I did not know until very recently was that she already had the heart disease of which she died in the mid-1940s, and that she had had suicides in her practice. One of the hazards and/or rewards of being a survivor is, incidentally, that one sometimes discovers, stumbles upon, information about one's analysts, that explains things about them that had previously been opaque. It was only when, a couple of years ago, I read Margaret Little's account of her own analysis with Ella Sharpe that I realised Sharpe had only been interested in the Oedipus complex and infantile sexuality, and that loss, bereavement, grief-subjects about which I then urgently needed enlightenment - did not enter into her theoretical scheme of things.

[[RunningHead]]

Mind and Body in Freud

David Smith

David Smith

Regent's Park, London NW1 4NS

David Smith  

There is a growing consensus amongst philosophers of mind and cognitive scientists that any psychology which can lay claim to being comprehensive must encompass mental processes themselves, the psychophysiological processes through which they are realised, and the relationship between mental processes and the external world as well as the relations between these three levels (Dennett 1978, 1987a, 1987b, Marr 1982, Newell 1980, 1982, Peacocke 1986, Pylyshyn 1984, Stabler 1983, Sterelny 1990). Any psychology which aspires to such comprehensiveness must face up to some profoundly philosophical questions.

The development of psychoanalysis is a good case in point. Sigmund Freud's neuroscientific education and his extensive clinical experience with hysteria made him particularly sensitive to the philosophical question of the relationship between mind and body. His eventual creation of psychoanalysis owes as much to Freud's philosophical preoccupations as it does to his experiences as a clinician.

It is widely believed that Freud began his scientific career as a hard-nosed materialist, and that his movement away from a materialistic stance coincided with his invention of psychoanalysis. According to this story Freud's early materialism was due to the baleful influence of his teachers (particularly Ernst Brücke), and his move away from this position was facilitated by his growing intellectual independence and striking clinical experiences which forced him to acknowledge the reciprocal relationship between body and mind.

There is a sense in which this story is true. Freud did grant increased scope to the mental. However, this story is more misleading than informative. Freud's intellectual and clinical struggles in the early 1890s led him to far-reaching reconsideration of his own philosophical position with respect to the mind-body problem. The consolidation of his views in 1895 coincided with the birth of psychoanalysis and to the abandonment of the concept of the mind which underpinned Studies on Hysteria (Smith 1992).

On Beginning Treatment

Charles Rycroft

Charles Rycroft

2 Modbury Gardens, London NW5 3QE

Charles Rycroft  

In ‘On Beginning Treatment’ I compare and contrast the ‘correct’ procedure for beginning an analysis that I was taught in the 1940s with how I begin treatment now in the 1990s. I argue that my present method is less rigid, less authoritarian and more realistic than the ‘classical’ procedure I was taught 50 years ago. I end the paper with some reflections on training analyses and their economic and emotional significance for both training analyst and trainee analysand.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Silence and Emptiness in the Service of Healing: Lessons from Meditation

Michael Monte

Michael Monte

St Patrick's Hospital, Dublin 8, Ireland

Michael Monte  

This article gives a brief historical introduction to meditation in the Christian and other religious traditions, relating it to concepts of Freud and Bion. Following a description of the technique of meditation, its essence is then discussed - especially in terms of its embeddedness in mystical traditions which hail from the old religions of the Orient. The main part of this paper concerns the work and teachings of John Main, the Benedictine monk who arguably did most to re-introduce the ancient discipline of Christian meditation to contemporary Western practitioners. Parallels are drawn between Main's view of silence in meditation and silence in psychoanalysis.

The article ends with some cautious notes on the possibility that meditation, as Main described it, may not be ideal for schizoid, dissociated, or overly narcissistic individuals. Those practitioners with good ego-strengths are likely to benefit the most.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

David Smith Replies

David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

Thank you for granting me the opportunity to respond to Mr Singh's recent letter. In spite of our sharp philosophical differences, Mr Singh and I possess something important in common. We are both concerned with the philosophical underpinnings of psychoanalysis and the intellectual status of psychoanalytic claims about mental life.

Although it may sound strange, I think that these philosophical issues should be of particular concern to clinicians. Psychoanalytic clinicians find themselves in a morally grave situation. If, as GrUnbaum and others claim, there are good reasons to doubt the veracity of the theories upon which psychoanalytic practice is based we are morally obliged to consider this deeply and seriously, to moderate our views accordingly and make sure that the public is aware of these reasonable doubts. Unfortunately, this is rather difficult to put into practice. The difficulty stems from the complex emotional relationship of psychoanalysts to their discipline, the autocratic and intellectually irresponsible attitudes of professional and training institutes, the absence of any tradition of institutionalised self-criticism within the profession and, last but not least, psychoanalysts' economic dependence upon the very ideas and methods upon which doubt is being cast. Notwithstanding the pervasive (and to my mind, selfcongratulatory) rhetoric of ‘not-knowing’ and ‘negative capability’, it seems to me that institutional psychoanalysis encourages doubt only within very narrow parameters. I think that this situation provides a rather telling example of the convergence of knowledge and human interests to which Mr Singh alludes in his letter. As Grunbaum (1993) himself puts it:

Very understandably, those who see their doctrine in jeopardy may find it more difficult to be receptive to my demurrer than it is for me to issue it… After all, whatever the fortunes of my polemic against Freud's clinical arguments and against post-Freudian variants on them (GrUnbaum, 1984, chap. 7) in the marketplace of ideas, my own professional craft as a philosopher is not put at risk by the outcome (xi).

[[RunningHead]]

Is Physics Really a Good Model for Psychoanalysis? Reflections on Langs and Badalamenti

Joseph Schwartz PHD

Joseph Schwartz

2 Lancaster Drive
London NW3 4HA

Joseph Schwartz  

Langs and Badalamenti (1994a) have given us a provocative account of their preliminary efforts to quantify the means by which therapists and clients express themselves in a psychoanalytic session. Using videotaped recordings of psychoanalytic consultations originally prepared for a teaching conference on how analysts work, Langs and Badalamenti have scored successive 8 second intervals* of the sessions according to five variables: how new is the material under discussion (newness of thematic material); to what extent a story is being told as opposed to generalisations being offered (extent of narration versus intellectualisation); to what extent the material is discussed in positive tones; to what extent in negative tones; and how halting or continuous the dialogue is.

In this way Langs and Badalamenti assemble a large database consisting of ten different time series, five for therapist and five for client. They approach their data in a number of different ways.

By calculating a standard statistical measure, the cross correlation between the time series of client and therapist, Langs and Badalamenti obtain measures of who follows whom in the session: if the therapist becomes more positively toned does the client follow? If the client becomes more positively toned does the therapist follow? In this sample of sessions the strongest correlations were observed in newness of theme, extent of narration and negative tone. The variances of these variables were also the largest. In two strongly experienced sessions the correlations in these variables along with their variances were both quite high, suggesting an attunement model of strong sessions where client and therapist are closely attuned (high correlations), and this attunement produces a wide range (large variance) of emotional response and newness of theme (spontaneity), all possible characteristics of what could be experienced as a strong session. Other interpretations are of course possible.

A second approach deals with just one of the time series, the continuity of dialogue. Here Langs and Badalamenti appear to have replicated a well-known effect in psychological linguistics - that the sound-silence patterns in monologues or dialogues when sampled at durations even as short as 300 milliseconds are well described by a type of coupled Poisson process, called a first order Markov chain, in which the distribution of both the lengths of utterances and of silences are decreasing exponentials (Jaffe et al. 1964). This is a worthwhile finding but its interpretation needs to be handled carefully.

[[RunningHead]]

The other Side of the Abyss: A Psychodynamic Approach to Working with Groups of People Who Came to England as Children on the Kindertransporte

Ruth Barnett

Ruth Barnett

31 Coleridge Walk, London NW11 6AT

Ruth Barnett  

This paper focuses on the psychological experience of children who were separated from their parents because they sent them to England to save their lives from the impending Holocaust in continental Europe. The parents of these children expressed their love and concern to ensure their offspring's survival through the self-sacrificial act of parting with them. What they could not prevent were the traumatic effects of this separation and its sequellae. Drawing on clinical material of former Kindertransportees as adults from her private practice and group work with a colleague, Ruth Barnett offers an understanding of the psychic journey that was imposed on these children by the deliberately inflicted atrocities to which their families and communities were subjected in the name of genocide and for the purpose of ‘ethnic cleansing’. She hopes this may be of some value to therapists working with the victims of similar attempts at ‘ethnic cleansing’ such as perpetrated in Rwanda and Bosnia.

Defensive Organizations or Collusive Interpretations? A Further Critique of Kleinian Theory and Practice

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

London SE1 9RT

Anthony Ryle  

A detailed commentary on a clinical study by O'Shaughnessy (1981) is presented from the viewpoint of the model of borderline personality developed in Cognitive Analytic Therapy. The delineation of separate ‘self states’, each with a characteristic repertoire of reciprocal roles, offers a different perspective on the pathology of the patient and on the impact of the analysis. On the basis of this and two previous papers it is argued that the status of defensive or pathological organizations is questionable and that the interpretations generated by Kleinian theory may exacerbate the patient's fragmentation.

[[RunningHead]]

The Inpatient Psychotherapy of a Mother and Child at the Cassel Hospital: A Case of Munchausen's Syndrome by Proxy

Paul Coombe

Paul Coombe

Melbourne, Victoria, Australia

Paul Coombe  

This account of the inpatient psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a mother and child at the Cassel Hospital, London is of a serious case of so-called ‘Munchausen's syndrome by proxy’. The mother presented two of her children to medical staff with complaints which were later found to be due to her chronic poisoning of them, by salt administration, which narrowly missed causing their death. It is an account of a treatment using both individual and group analytic methods in a psychoanalytic therapeutic community. Attention is drawn to the mother's use of projective identification defensively and malignantly in a concrete fashion and its gradual conversion into a more benign agent. The function of the institution as a container is described, and comment is made on the experience of working with severe cases of child abuse.

[[RunningHead]]

Cross-Gender Identifications in Heterosexual Couples

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

TMSI, Tavistock Centre
120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Warren Colman  

A well-established sense of gender does not depend on sexual object choice but on a sense of security in belonging to the gender correlated to one's biological sex. Cross-gender identifications are often found in heterosexual couples who show a marked reversal of conventional gender norms and whose typical interaction constitutes a shared defence against their mutual lack of gender security. Both partners are ‘possessed’ by the contrasexual archetype (anima and animus) and have been unable to integrate their contrasexual potential. Three aetiological factors seem to predispose both men and women towards cross-gender identification: an over-close relationship with the parent of the opposite sex, a negative identification with the parent of the same sex and inappropriate use by their mothers as substitute caretakers (‘narcissistic objects’). In both sexes masculinity is idealised while femininity is denigrated.

responseSet.title: Introduction
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction

Juliet Mitchell

Juliet Mitchell

USA

Juliet Mitchell  

I don't know what we represent on the panel, except long friendship and interests, both on the theoretical side of psychoanalysis and in its clinical practice, and by now a long history of feminism together. Though we have been out of touch on and off as individuals during the last 20 years we all feel very pleased to remeet. But the panel is not just based on friendship; we thought that in some ways we represent the different ways in which people have taken an interest in psychoanalysis and feminism in the last 20 years. So that where my book was really exclusively relating to issues of patriarchy and heterosexuality, Joanna Ryan has taken it into the diversity of women/women relationships. Margot Waddell has from the beginning been involved in working with children and adolescents, and women and children, and women and adolescents, and girls becoming women and feminism in relation to that. Joan Raphael-Leff has worked with issues of reproduction and motherhood; so that we all felt we opened up four of the different ways psychoanalysis has been taken.

To begin I thought I would do a rough synopsis of the history of why it all happened. But I also have one question to address to the plenary this afternoon and this is, why are we all here? Beyond my pleasure and my intense anxiety about such a large audience, I am really genuinely very puzzled. I mean, where are we coming from? Are we interested in psychoanalysis, or feminism, or both? If we are feminists, why aren't we elsewhere as well as here? Why isn't more happening outside where I'm longing to see myself as well as everybody else here? Every day I feel an absence of us, in the field, so to speak. So while it is an enormous pleasure which I in no way want to detract from, I would like us also to bear that question in mind. Can we also be elsewhere in some sort of way, at some very near future point?

That, in a way, is really where I want to start, because my own book and the work of others on psychoanalysis and feminism, at the end of the sixties, came out of the exigency of the political situation. It was not a theoretical question, it was not an academic issue, it was not a clinical issue. It was a political need that produced our work, and certainly produced my own books. And my particular book, Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974), was not a monument to anything, but a part of a political struggle. That's really very much how it was; in an atmosphere in which it was part of a debate, part of a political need, that women had in the sixties. I still want to address that need because psychoanalysis and feminism may not be the answer. The need is, I think, still with us; perhaps as it is part of the answer, and there are ways in which we can still take it. That is what we are here to discuss today.

Holmes on Bowlby and the Future of Psychotherapy: A Response

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

SE1 9RT

Anthony Ryle  

Holmes' discussion of the clinical implications of attachment theory is critically discussed. It is argued that the use of interpretation presented by Holmes to explain Bowlby's dispute with the psychoanalytic establishment is inappropriate and that the differences between psychoanalytic ideas and those proposed by Bowlby and arising from later observational studies of early development are substantial. Finally it is suggested that neither Bowlby nor psychoanalysis pay sufficient attention to the child's organisation of meaning in the early interaction with caretakers.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Does Psychotherapy Need ‘NVQs’?

Rosemary Randall

Rosemary Randall

113 Gwydir St, Cambridge CB1 2LG

Rosemary Randall  

Anyone who visits a professional person hopes that he or she will be competent at what they do. The more astute or anxious may enquire about qualifications, find out about people's trainings, ask for recommendations and compare notes with friends. Certainly, members of the public have a right to expect that psychotherapists will be competent to practise psychotherapy and to expect there to be professional bodies that can control the quality of training, enforce standards and provide redress in the case of incompetent or unprofessional behaviour. This is the rationale for the existence of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy.

Competent in this sense, however, is a far cry from the so-called ‘competencies’ that we are currently being asked to consider as a possible framework for training and practice, and I think the profession would do well to examine further the philosophy and assumptions that lie behind them. These competencies are proposed as the key element of a National Vocational Qualification (NVQ) that would guarantee common standards of training and practice across the profession (The Advice, Guidance & Counselling Lead Body 1993). Currently drafted for counselling (including psychodynamic counselling) it is proposed to extend them to include psychotherapy. They are offered as neutral descriptions, as a process of mapping that we can contribute to and as an open participatory framework that will benefit public and profession alike. I argue in this article that they are not neutral. I believe that they propound a philosophy that is alien to psychoanalytic psychotherapy and that, if extended to include psychotherapy, they would initiate changes in the training and practice of psychotherapy that would benefit neither the public nor the profession. (The Draft Standards for counselling that I refer to in this article have been amended following consultation and are now published in a final version [April 1995]. Although some changes have been made, their overall approach and philosophy is unaltered.)

An Analysis of Intellectual Dysfunction

Robert Royston

Robert Royston

25 Dalmeny Road, London N7

Robert Royston  

Thinking inhibitions may affect a person's academic and professional performance and damage aesthetic enjoyment. They can emerge in the analytic encounter as an inability to digest interpretive ideas and insights. The present paper describes the experience of intellectual blocking and offers a theory to account for the psychodynamics and causes. The argument is traced through three case studies, using an object relations theoretical approach that is distinguished from some other psychoanalytic viewpoints.

Jale Punter  

The results of an audit project on treatment length from an NHS department of psychoanalytic psychotherapy are outlined. Average lengths of treatment in individual and group therapy are reported. responseSet.title: What's Happening to Mourning?
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

What's Happening to Mourning?

Ian Craib

Ian Craib

Colchester, Essex C04 3SQ

Ian Craib  

The paper attempts to show the way in which psychotherapy can become caught up in wider social processes that change the meaning of psychotherapeutic work in a way of which we are not always aware. The process of mourning is taken as an example; the classic theories of mourning are examined and the way they have changed over the last thirty years is discussed. It is argued that the changes have been a product of social change rather than a deeper understanding of grief, and that unless we are aware of this, psychotherapy can turn into an instrument of social control.

responseSet.title: Editorial
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Often in our professional discussions recently, it seems there is a tendency to alight on the element of envious destructiveness as the keystone to emotional disorder, no matter what our theoretical orientation. This can sometimes sound like a one-noted trumpet that might obscure other important emotional states needing attention. Shame is basic to our experience of being human, but perhaps we have not fully recognised the importance of its undertones. Malcolm Pines writes of the various aspects of shame and how sensitive handling of it in psychotherapy can release affect and strengthen the self. In a different vein, we try never to underestimate the importance of mourning, but has it undergone a sea change in post-modern culture? Ian Craib rebukes the therapeutic community for what he sees as a formulaic approach, distorting the mourning process and over-socialising the individual away from the full implication of loss. David Malan does not quite agree with Ian Craib, and gives here his Response. Turning to the phenomena of silence and emptiness, we see that they can have quite different meanings from the point of view of other disciplines, and yet be related to and contribute to our understanding of the way the mind works: Michael Del Monte provides an illuminating guide to meditation practices.

The Student Essay First Prize for 1994 went to Francis Grier, whose paper might be described as variations on theoretical themes, how they can work together to enhance each other, and how they can firmly structure once-a-week work. He finds Kleinian theory most useful for understanding defensive and communicative systems, and Fairbairnian theory best for contemplating the inner world. He relates the internal saboteur to Bion's and Rosenfeld's psychotic part of the personality, an inner force that prevents libidinal attachments.

The Joint Conference held by the BJP and the Freud Museum in February 1994 - ‘Hysteria Today: 100 Years since Freud’- was a successful event indicating the keen interest in hysteria that is still with us. This issue contains three previously unpublished papers from the conference by David Smith, Ann Scott and Estela Welldon. On 14 May 1995, another joint conference with the Freud Museum will be held on a topic of central concern in psychoanalytic thought -‘How do we think about feelings?’ (see p. 378, this issue, for more details). The speakers will include André Green, Eric Rayner, Luis Rodriguez de la Sierra, Rosine Perelberg and David Bell. We look forward to this event, hoping that it will be received as enthusiastically as the 1994 Annual Lecture last Autumn. The Annual Lecture is commented upon in the Correspondence section in this issue in a letter from Jo Klein. More correspondence from Neville Singh and David Smith pivots around the scientific vs the interpretative view of psychoanalysis, based on Grunbaum's criticisms. As clinicians, hearing these arguments, we can try to be clear about where we stand in terms of our philosophical position, as David Smith urges.
