responseSet.title: Response to Ian Craib's ‘What's Happening to Mourning?’
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Response to Ian Craib's ‘What's Happening to Mourning?’

David Malan

David Malan

Parker's Close, Hartley Wintney, Hants RG27 8JG

David Malan  

I think the central point that Ian Craib is trying to make is the danger of losing sight of both the individuality, the pain, and the depth of the process of mourning. Put like that the point is valid.

The trouble is that his views are so extreme. The article reads as if he believes this criticism applies to all psychotherapy, including psychoanalysis, which obviously is not true. If he spelled out more clearly that he is concerned with a trend in certain areas of society and psychotherapy, the article would be much more acceptable.

There is also a faintly paranoid atmosphere to what he says. Thus he accuses Abraham, who merely pointed out that internalisation of the loved one was part of normal mourning, of trying to ‘establish the mourning process as an area of professional expertise and control’. Freud, Abraham, and Klein ‘illustrate a process of a profession carving out an area of power for itself,’… the psychiatric profession and then the therapy and counselling professions have attempted to establish control over mourning' - not that they are trying to extend the use of their skills to help a group of people in need. When Parkes writes of trying to deal with emotions (rather than the patient's inner world), Craib says, ‘We are moving closer to quasi-behaviourism’ - surely the one thing behaviourism does not deal with is emotions. He quotes a recent handbook which states the aims of bereavement counselling as (1) to help resolve bereavement, (2) to prevent ‘malresolution’, and (3) to resolve malresolution if it has happened, and then writes contemptuously, ‘The job becomes getting the machine back on the road’. I would have thought that these three aims were absolutely impeccable, and that most severely depressed people would come to a therapist with the hope of becoming able to live a normal life again - rather than have their own lives and those of everyone close to them disrupted or destroyed. Craib is also contemptuous of searching for effective methods of therapy which ‘only’ enable the patient to find creativity and happiness, labelling this as ‘selling goods on a market to attract customers or to please management’ - again, I would have thought most patients would settle for creativity and happiness as the outcome of their therapy.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

History of the British Confederation of Psychotherapists

Fred Balfour and Joscelyn Richards

Joscelyn Richards

37a Mapesbury Road, London NW2 4HJ

Joscelyn Richards  

The Editor of the British Journal of Psychotherapy asked the BCP Council if we would like to write an article about the history of the Confederation to accompany Michael Pokorny's history of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP). We were pleased to accept the invitation as both umbrella organisations have their roots in the publication of the Foster Report of 1971. That Report was the outcome of a government-commissioned investigation carried out by Sir John Foster. The Report recommended that, for the protection of the public, psychotherapists in the United Kingdom should be registered. Subsequently a Professions Joint Working Party, chaired by Paul Sieghart, was established to develop in more detail the proposals of the Foster Report. A number of the BCP member organisations were members of that Working Party. A Report was published in 1978 which also recommended a statutory scheme of regulation for psychotherapists in order ‘to protect the public from unscrupulous or incompetent practitioners’. For many reasons no British government has wanted to introduce statutory legislation of psychotherapists but the present government has encouraged voluntary registration. One of the consequences of all these developments is that both the UKCP and the BCP are now publishing registers.

In many ways the UKCP has attempted to do something more complex and difficult than the BCP: it has attempted to form a structure which encompasses a large range of psychotherapies, both well established at the time of the Foster Report and newly developed since then. This has been an admirable undertaking and we have already congratulated the UKCP on their achievements in bringing some cohesion to a fragmented field.

However, a sign that in the long term the impressively plural field of psychotherapy was likely to need to be contained in more than a single national register occurred prior to the establishment of the UKSCP (United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy), now the UKCP. The Working Party of the then Rugby Conference, the UKSCP's precursor, had been set the task by the Conference to advise it about its future structure. That Working Party suggested the creation of a container organisation which encompassed the diversity of institutions involved while differentiating titles and functions as appropriately as possible.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy: A Profession for Troubled Times

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith

NW1 4NS

Emmy van Deurzen-Smith  

UKCP has been concerned about European regulations for psychotherapy for a number of years. At the end of the eighties it became clear that there was a risk that the profession would become regulated through the European Commission in Brussels if a sectoral directive were to be put into place. There were fears that such a directive would jeopardise the independence of the profession of psychotherapy as we know it in Britain and that it would regulate it as a specialism of medicine or psychology instead.

In pursuing independence of the psychotherapy profession UKCP became actively involved in the creation of a European Association for Psychotherapy sponsored by the Dutch Psychotherapy Association (NVP) in Amsterdam in 1990. For various reasons this organisation did not live up to its original promise and UKCP withdrew its support and joined the Vienna-based European Association for Psychotherapy in 1993. The EAP is an organisation sponsored by the Austrian Psychotherapy Association and now has members from over 20 European countries. It is based on the Strasbourg Declaration for Psychotherapy which states categorically that psychotherapy is an independent and scientifically based profession. Its aims and objectives are eminently compatible with those of UKCP.

In 1992, after several visits to the Commission, UKCP was invited by the DTI to send an expert to a decisive meeting of the coordinators of the Directive on Higher Degrees and Diplomas, which regulates all professions that do not have a sectoral directive. At this meeting at the European Commission psychotherapy regulation across the European Union was discussed and it was decided that for the time being it would be unsuitable to regulate psychotherapy in any other way than by mutual recognition through the general directive.

It was also agreed that the subject of psychotherapy would be discussed again as soon as regulation would have been achieved in a number of countries and enough information about the profession in the different countries of the EU was available. This gave us a breathing space in which to organise ourselves. It was evident that it would be important to work directly through a European organisation to secure a broadly based and independent psychotherapy profession across the European Union. There were several countries, such as Italy, the Netherlands and Germany, where legislation regulating psychotherapy as a specialisation of medicine and psychology was in place or underway.

[[RunningHead]]

The Rhetorical Voice of Psychoanalysis: Displacement of Evidence by Theory by Donald P. Spence. Published by Harvard University Press, Cambridge, Mass. and London, 1994; 228 pages.

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

British Psycho-Analytical Society, London

Andrea Sabbadini  

The Rhetorical Voice of Psychoanalysis is an ambitious, often powerful, but ultimately unsatisfactory critique of psychoanalysis. It is a telling detail that the blurb of this book should describe its American author, Donald P. Spence, as ‘Professor of Psychiatry’ without referring to the fact that he is also a psychoanalyst.

Spence views contemporary psychoanalysis as a monolithic body of theory and practice and assumes that nothing has substantially changed in the analytic world since its early days. He feels therefore free to use repeated attacks on Freud - his discovery of the Oedipus complex (‘a tragedy’), his use of metaphors, his self-analysis (‘a legend’) and his (‘misleading’) case histories - to undermine psychoanalysis as it is practised today. This seems an unfair approach as the claim of a ‘troubling lack of progress’ (p. 1) in analytic theory and technique remains unsubstantiated. The same applies to the statement that ‘once Freud had made up his mind, he was unusually resistant to changing it’ (pp. 104-105), while in fact Freud repeatedly reviewed his own metapsychology, e.g. by abandoning the seduction hypothesis, postulating the death drive, replacing the topographical with the structural model and introducing a new theory of anxiety.

Spence sees psychoanalysis as being committed to an in-depth study of individual specimen - be they the dream of the botanical monograph in Die Traumdeutung or the clinical case of Dora - following the Aristotelian conceptualist model, as well as the Romantic idealisation of the explorer of far-away lands and the archaeologist of deep-buried cities. This tendency is contrasted by Spence with the more respectable Baconian and Galilean traditions, prevalent in modern natural sciences, that favour strictly observed empirical methodologies involving quantitative research, controlled experiments, the build-up of a database of records and consensual validation.

The problem is the author's own ambiguous position in relation to these two apparently incompatible epistemolological models, already present in the ambivalence of his sympathy for the hermeneutic approach to psychoanalysis in his acclaimed previous book Narrative Truth and Historical Truth (1982). He is not quite suggesting here that psychoanalysis should entirely operate in the inductive tradition - after all, how could (and why should) therapists quantify the subjective human experiences that are the very stuff of their enquiry? But Spence believes, and I agree with him here, that our discipline cannot pretend to belong to that scientific tradition, while in fact operating in the Aristotelian mode and thus speaking with what he calls ‘a rhetorical voice’.

Attachment Processes in Adulthood (Volume 5 of Advances in Personal Relationships) edited by Kim Bartholomew and Daniel Perlman. Published by Jessica Kingsley, London, 1992; 342 pages.

Tirril Harris

Tirril Harris

LCP, BAP, London

Tirril Harris  

One of the saddest aspects of recent developments in psychoanalytic thought has been that its main protagonists often seem unaware of its impact on other disciplines. As a result, in their turn, the workers in these other disciplines are never obliged to communicate more broadly and lapse into ever more specialised jargon of their own. Bartholomew and Perlman's book, based entirely on a theoretical framework developed by a psychoanalyst but couched in terms of academic social science, is one example-of this gulf between groups of allied thinkers. And yet anyone who believes in object-relations theory ought to be grateful to the growing body of academic research workers who seek to make it scientifically testable, and whose concerns therefore involve the intricacies of data collection, measurement systems, reliability and validity. This volume, the fifth in a series on personal relationships, is devoted to John Bowlby's attachment theory and details recent developments in methodology and aetiological research in this field. These features are dealt with clearly and thoroughly but, in the absence of specific subheadings on therapeutic outcome, few psychotherapists will find the motivation to burrow away among the worthy statistics in order to locate the gems of insight which exist among the findings.

The book has four main themes: conceptualisation/measurement, developmental aspects, applications to adult couples, and conceptual extensions of attachment theory to the fields of coping with stress, caregiving (as well as receiving) and religious belief. While the first part is invaluable in its exposition of Bowlby's basic theory of ‘internal working models of relationships’ it is also the part most devoted to academic discussion of methodological issues.

Part two provides more substance. First the Steeles report on the London Parent-Child Project, which revealed the close connections between the attachment style of mothers interviewed in late pregnancy about their childhood relationships with their own parents, and the security of their one-year-old infants after a brief separation in the laboratory some fifteen months later. In concluding, they mention a preventive intervention study with anxiously attached mother-child dyads which succeeded in reducing insecurity among the infants between ages one and two. Part two continues with chapters on conversation and adolescent security and on the integration of sexuality with attachment. The latter may be difficult to grapple with for those of us strictly reared in the traditional psychoanalytic model, but such thought-provoking pieces can promote important reassessments.

Existential Psychotherapy and the Interpretation of Dreams by Clark Moustakas. Published by Jason Aronson Inc., Northvale, New Jersey, 1994; 219 pages.

Hans Cohn

Hans Cohn

Regent's College, London

Hans Cohn  

The word ‘existential’, increasingly used to characterise an approach to psychotherapy different from or even opposed to the psychodynamic model, can mean many things.

485

At times it only gives an emotional colouring to whatever it describes: if it is ‘existential’, it is ‘profound’ or ‘ultimate’. At others it implies that the concern is ‘man's existence’-but in such a general sense, is this not the concern of any kind of psychotherapy?

It is frequently forgotten that there is a philosophical orientation, existentialism (or more correctly, existential phenomenology), represented particularly by the philosophers, Heidegger, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty. In their writings ‘existence’ has a specific meaning, describing the way in which human beings are ‘in the world’, a world that defines them as it is defined by them. Exploration of the phenomenon ‘existence’ reveals its temporal limitation, the fact that a great deal of it is outside our control, is given, but that we have the freedom to choose our response to what there is though the outcome of our choices is never certain. This freedom is double-faced: it is a threat and a potentiality. Anxiety is an inevitable aspect of this uncertainty.

These are the basic existential themes. There is also a history and tradition of existential psychotherapy which is essentially Central European. The Swiss psychoanalyst Medard Boss, in spite of a great admiration for Freud's therapeutic methods, found the physicalistic theory underlying them unsatisfactory. The Swiss psychiatrist Ludwig Binswanger drew Boss's attention to the writings of Heidegger. Both Binswanger and Boss rethought their ideas about psychological disturbance in the light of Heidegger's philosophy. Boss became a friend of Heidegger, and the extensive discussion of psychotherapeutic concepts between a psychoanalyst and one of the originators of existential philosophy led to the development of a school of existential psychotherapy called Daseinsanalyse (analysis of being-there). Boss's book Psychoanalysis and Daseinsanalysis, which appeared in 1964 in the States, is a comprehensive attempt to provide psychoanalytic practice with a philosophical (rather than a scientific) basis.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 75, 677, 1994

The Value of the Historical Perspective to Contemporary Psychoanalysis: Freud's ‘Seduction Hypothesis’

Rachel B. Blass and Bennett Simon

In this paper the authors re-examine the development of Freud's ideas on seduction, with a special focus on the evidence which Freud presented and upon which he relied as he attempted to confirm these ideas. Through this re-examination Freud's struggle with seductiveness, both in relation to his patients and in relation to his theories, comes to the fore. While the wish to be with the other through exerting an influence over him or her is perverted in the act of sexual seduction, it is, nevertheless, a force that must be recognised and contended with in other creative interchanges, including the analytic one. In studying Freud's struggle with this force, there is attained a better appreciation of the humanness, including the inevitable human limitations, of Freud and his thinking that rest at the foundation of psychoanalysis. This study thus has clear implications for the history of psychoanalysis, but, more importantly, it reveals the value for contemporary psychoanalysis in recognising this history.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 75, 743, 1994

Psychoanalysis as a Lifeline: A Clinical Study of a Transference Perversion

Ronald Baker

Case material from the analysis of a fetishistic cross-dresser is reported. The evolution of a transference perversion and treatment impasse, in the form of the recalcitrant symptom of anal flatulence, is described. The patient's contrasting needs to cling perversely and addictively to the analyst, on the one hand, and to provoke an acting out of the countertransference, on the other, are placed in the context of his dread of rejection and potentially suicidal reaction. The author argues in favour of offering psychoanalysis as a lifeline, but with the condition that the psychoanalytic setting and boundaries are maintained and that gratifications are denied. Limited but precise interpretive psychoanalytic work in the transference was maintained. The relatively good outcome is explained in terms of the provision of safety, survival of the analyst and avoidance of countertransference acting out, which, in the author's view, represents an implicit and mutative transference interpretation, the specific factor in bringing about psychic change. This enabled the patient to recognise and accept the analyst as a ‘new’ object and, as a consequence, to question and reject his idealisation of the anal universe that he inhabited.

Psychoanalysis, Cognitive-Analytic Therapy, Mind and Self

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

Introduction

As readers of the Journal will know, the Annual Lecture is an occasion which brings together a guest speaker and our community of readers, editorial board members, and essay prize winners. 1994's Lecture, which marked the Journal's first 10 years, was something of a departure in two respects. It extended a debate which had been taking place in the Journal, and it took the form of a joint presentation.

By way of background, the starting-point was a paper by Anthony Ryle: a provocative critique of Betty Joseph's ‘Addiction to near-death’ from a cognitiveanalytic therapy perspective (BJP 10(1)1993), with my short response in the same issue and a further response by Dr Ryle (BJP 10(3) 1994). In a style designed to stimulate debate Dr Ryle was challenging a number of key assumptions about the approach to treatment, and to the treatment alliance, that stemmed, as he saw it, from a particular Kleinian model of the mind; he was also posing questions about the treatment of borderline personality disorder within and outside the public sector. How effective is long-term work? Can severe psychopathology be treated with the shorter-term therapies favoured in the public sector? How are resources best and most fairly deployed? For many these are questions of the greatest urgency.

The 1994 Lecture was planned during Bob Hinshelwood's last year as Editor, and with Jean Arundale's involvement as Editor-Elect the idea of extending the debate by inviting Peter Fonagy to speak together with Dr Ryle was arrived at. As Freud Memorial Professor of Psychoanalysis at University College London, Peter Fonagy is working on developing the theory of psychoanalysis, including its ideas of the self. He too has a particular interest in the conceptualization and treatment of borderline states.

The format proved a successful one: as Jean Arundale said in her opening remarks, the two lecturers could ‘speak to each other, and relate to each other's ideas’. Readers will be able to track that process in what follows. The immediacy of the issues at stake, both practically and theoretically, is captured by both speakers. In addition, the quality of the discussion was such that it seemed important to include it along with the lectures; it is reproduced here in full.

Commentary by a Child Psychotherapist from the Anna Freud Centre

Tessa Baradon

Tessa Baradon

Anna Freud Centre
21 Maresfield Gardens
London NW3 5SH

Tessa Baradon  

This commentary incorporates a lively discussion that took place in our Clinical Research Group at the Anna Freud Centre.

Responding to a clinical session is always a challenge. Processes are clear in hindsight but the session reflects the therapist's attempts to respond ‘on her toes’ to what is taking place in the analytic space. To do this she capitalises on the relationship and course of work that have been established. But these are unknown to the readers in these clinical commentaries. Therefore this kind of summary gives rise to many questions and fantasies in the commentator. These will influence the way we look at the session and I will therefore spell them out.

John presents a discontinuity of experience with regards to himself and to the object. From her reported responses to him, I understand that the therapist has formulated the child's problem in terms of fragmentation and sees him as a child who cannot hold an integrated object in mind. It seems to me that this frame of reference defined her verbal responses in their session. On the other hand, my impression is that the therapist is warm and caring towards this vulnerable child, and that her affective attitude held the session together. I thought the child was responding to this in his non-verbal engagement with her.

Indeed I noted that at 18 months, an important age in terms of the capacity to integrate and symbolise, this child's life fell apart. I wonder how far his internal experience of discontinuity is related to the epilepsy, as a constitutional problem or, perhaps and, reactive to it. With this in mind we could view the child accruing experiences of non-chiming with the object around the epileptic episodes, with the object continuing to behave while he was ‘absent’ from the interaction during the fit.

Valli Kohon

Valli Kohon

44 Fitzjohn's Avenue
London NW3 5LX

Valli Kohon  

The session is dominated by the theme of transition. Transition between the outside and inside of a session, between one person and another, one place, experience and

609

state of mind and another. In the session John and his therapist explore John's infancy and his present age, and the transitions between sessions and terms of therapy.

In a general way, the session made me think about the brief history the therapist gives us at the beginning. John might have experienced a confusing and persecuting sense of loss of his mother both during and after her pregnancy with Mark; it seems that the session illustrates his struggle to understand what happened.

Despite John's developmental delay, he is a child with a wish to use his mind to think with, and to acquire a clearer idea of the sequence of important events in his life. He alternates between a more mature aspect of himself, asking questions and wanting to clarify things, and a more regressive baby-like aspect wanting the comfort of a pillow and blanket and playing a peep-bo game. In his communication he uses words and language to try to understand, and at the same time plays games that symbolise his experience of loss (such as the telephone and peep-bo). I was struck by John's inclination to talk rather than play, as if he were holding onto the more mature element in himself in his attempt to make sense of things.

In the waiting-room John's father expresses mock despair. Without knowing the nature of the therapist's relationship with the parents, this expression suggests the father's wish to engage in his own dialogue with the therapist, leaving John outside their interaction. It might indicate the ongoing burden of looking after John, showing how difficult it is for the father to stay in contact with his son. John's grin seems anxious, particularly because of the way he drops everything to engage with the therapist, the anxiety being quickly carried over into the flicking of his hands, as if he is letting go of his father and quickly needs to grasp the next person within reach.

Frances Tustin: Makers of Modern Psychotherapy by Sheila Spensley. Published by Routledge, London, 1995; 154 pages; £12.99.

Pauline Josefowitz

Pauline Josefowitz

ACP, London

Pauline Josefowitz  

This clear and dense book appears as part of a series of ‘introductory critical texts’, entitled Makers of Modern Psychotherapy. Its publication so soon after Frances Tustin's death in November 1994 is to be welcomed not only by those interested in learning about her life and work but by those who are mourning the loss of a most original thinker, an inspiring teacher, supervisor, colleague and beloved friend.

In the introduction, Spensley defines her objectives: ‘This book is about the distinguished contribution to the psychoanalytic investigation of Autism which Frances Tustin has made’ (p. 1). On the following page she specifies that she is also interested in the ‘reassessment of the tenuous links first observed between autism and psychosis with the aim more of illuminating psychosis than autism’ (p. 2). She thus indicates that her interests are twofold, and that the book will offer more than its title may suggest.

The first two biographical chapters give a lively, insightful account of Frances Tustin's religious family background, childhood, studies and training as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic. The different influences and experiences that led to her ‘discovery of autism’ (p. 20) and the publication of her first book Autism and Childhood Psychosis in 1972 are described. However, Spensley's account of Tustin's life and work ends at this point, and one has to consult the chronology and the bibliography at the end of the book to find out about the titles of her three subsequent books as well as the existence of the many articles and papers that she wrote. She concludes the biographical part of the book with some equivocal remarks about this time being ‘a critical period in Tustin's life when her relationships were in turmoil. She had left her analyst; she had left the Tavistock Child Guidance Centre; she had left the workshop which Meltzer had set up for the study of autism; and she had moved out of London’ (p. 19). The reader, who might be using Spensley's book as an introduction to Tustin's life and work, may be left, not only somewhat confused about the nature and meaning of these events, but also in the dark about Tustin's later years. No mention is made, for instance, of her ever-growing recognition as a world authority on autism or of the rare honour bestowed upon her when she was appointed Honorary Affiliate by the British Society of Psycho-Analysis in 1984.

Eric Rhode

Eric Rhode

ACP, London

Eric Rhode  

He started off in a direction quite contrary to that of the question, as if in retreat from the aggressive intent, then made a wide sweep, ending by taking the enemy, not even on the flank, but from the rear … He seemed often to tap the wording to see if the vocabulary of the question rang true or seemed soft at the centre. Then he probed it for preconceptions, leading qualities, various penumbra of meaning from common parlance. Then often came a kind of

622

brutal thumping of its presumption that an answer existed as the malheur de la question. And, finally, he attacked it as a problem related to the central question of the meaning of psychoanalysis as a thing-in-itself.

This is Donald Meltzer sharing his delight in W.R. Bion's powers as a conversationalist. Its humour is typical - and is bound up with courage as the other quality essential to the possibility of deepening states of an intimacy, which Donald Meltzer relates to certain conceptions of nurture and family life, and which is an abiding preoccupation in his psychoanalytic writings.

Throughout the 34 remarkable papers that make up this book the issue recurs of how to deepen the intimacy of the therapeutic couple and to realise the meaning of the loneliness that is intimacy's converse, without being destroyed or betrayed by human inadequacy in the face of unpredictable feeling. Titles like ‘Narcissistic foundation of the erotic transference’ or ‘The role of pregenital confusions in erotomania’ describe the dangers. One paper in particular, ‘Routine and inspired interpretations: their relation to the weaning process in analysis’, deals with the issue in a manner that still belongs to the future. Writing of this kind results in insights that are quite raw. Of a schizophrenic youth (about whom he has written elsewhere) Donald Meltzer says, ‘the degree of his enslavement to an internal persecutor could be fairly judged by the distance his hand was withdrawn up his shirt-sleeve’.

Donald Meltzer has characterised courage in therapy as allowing oneself to be a mind unveiled, the emperor without clothes as in the Hans Christian Andersen story. It is plain that only one child has the guilelessness openly to recognise the emperor's candour; everybody else ridicules the emperor, or is worried on his behalf. The emperor's courage in allowing himself to be as naked as the first couple certainly requires that he should be able gently to see himself as an object of humour.

Phil Mollon  

This is the nearest to a biography of Kohut that is currently available, and provides not only a fascinating portrait of the man but also of his time and culture and of the place of psychoanalysis within that. We see the optimism of the New World, and of Kohut as a new migrant to it, the early vision of analysis as providing an understanding and perhaps solutions to man's problems, and generally the sense that the American Way was essentially correct; all of which appears as if of another and more naive era as we approach the millennium. Will there still be something called psychoanalysis in the twenty-first century?

Kohut was born in 1913, the year Freud wrote ‘On narcissism’, the paper which spawned much of Kohut's later theorising. He died in 1981. Like Freud, Kohut fled from Vienna to escape the Nazis. He arrived in Chicago as a young doctor and after an analysis with Ruth Eissler- which cost him $1200 per year out of a salary of $3000 - he rapidly became established in the 1950s as a leading figure in the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute and eventually became President of the APA.

Kohut's reformulations of narcissism, which led to his development of ‘self psychology’, began in the mid-1960s, the major controversies being played out during the 1970s.

Seductive Mirage: An Exploration of the Work of Sigmund Freud by Allen Esterson. Published by Open Court, Chicago, 1993; 270 pages; £14.95 (paperback).

David Smith

David Smith

London

David Smith  

Sigmund Freud's work - his theories, clinical techniques and methodological norms - are crucial to the field of psychoanalysis. Allen Esterson's book is an important contribution to that stream of recent Freud scholarship which casts doubt on the coherence, plausibility and integrity of many aspects of Freud's work. Seductive Mirage is clearly written and conscientiously researched. Esterson goes through a number of Freud's texts, noting contradictions both within and between them. He argues that these contradictions are, on the whole, symptoms of Freud's efforts to place himself and his work in an unjustifiably favourable light. Perhaps more significantly, Esterson points out the dire consequences of Freud's systematic blurring of the distinction between observation and inference, a tendency which provides many of his accounts with spurious authority. Esterson's discussion of Freud's ‘seduction theory’ is a particularly fine example of this type of analysis.

There are, however, three aspects of the book with which I am uncomfortable. Firstly, Esterson does not normally refer back to the German text when he spots an apparent contradiction in Freud, i.e. he does not routinely entertain the possibility that such contradictions might on some occasions be translator's artefacts. Secondly, in his enthusiasm for debunking Freud, Esterson does not often consider how textual contradictions might be resolved more charitably. Exegesis is a subtle business. Sometimes we cannot square things because we do not have a sufficiently complex grasp of the issues. A good example of this is the scholarly debate about the originality (or otherwise) of Freud's concept of the unconscious. It is perfectly true, as Esterson, Whyte, Ellenberger and others have claimed, that the notion of unconscious states was topical in the late nineteenth century. But it is also true that the term ‘unconscious’ is ambiguous and was used to denote a multitude of conceptions. Some authors, for example, used the term ‘unconscious ideas’ to denote neurophysiological states which give rise to conscious ideas. Some took it to refer to dissociated aspects of consciousness. Others used it to denote ‘weak’ ideas (hypothesising that consciousness is a function of the causal power of a mental content), while still others used ‘unconscious’ to denote all mental states under neurophysiological descriptions. Freud himself used the term ‘unconscious’ in several distinct senses, and it is not always easy to discern his meaning in any given passage. Thirdly, it is not always clear to what extent Freud's errors (as understood from a contemporary perspective) were, in fact, errors in the context of the methodological norms of his intellectual culture.

Carol Topolski

Carol Topolski

BAP, London

Carol Topolski  

Body politic, body beautiful, body talk, body of evidence, good body, bad body, the first ego is a body ego - we inhabit our own bodies, we experience the bodies of others, we ‘know’ carnally, but what would it be, to hate and abuse the body that houses us? Each of these books looks with its particular eye at the late twentieth-century phenomena of eating disorders, which are burgeoning particularly in the rich soil of the industrialised Northern hemisphere. Not that eating disorders are new: Understanding Eating Disorders points to the case of Frederada, a serf in the ninth century, who would ‘eat like a cow’, then utterly refuse food, and whose fixed obsessional character traits closely resembled the clinical picture of anorexia nervosa appearing in consulting rooms today. Not until 1980, however, did anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa become enshrined as separate syndromes in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM III), so focusing thinking on the experience, meaning and treatment of these disorders that wrack and ravage the body with the turmoils of the mind.

Each book speaks with a different tongue, although hung around the same central thematic post: Understanding Eating Disorders, its cover littered with weighty numbers, speaks the language of science, of research and critique, of measuring and concluding, whilst The Good Body with its velvet cover bearing a woman's form, is polyglottal, as philosophers, anthropologists, literary scholars and historians ruminate on what it is to have a body in contemporary culture. The one is an investigation, the other, a meditation.

Understanding Eating Disorders presents its menu in ordered form: an historical introduction, together with general and particular commentary on the developmental, familial and abusive aspects of these disorders, followed by sections on each of three syndromes: anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and obesity. In contrast, The Good Body finds the syndromes in the cross-hatching of different spotlights: as a ‘postmodern reappearance of gnostic isolation’, as a ‘cultural management of female desire and female flight from a purely reproductive destiny’, as a perverse pleasure, both as sedition and conformity. Minuchin and Mahler appear as informants in Understanding Eating Disorders, Aristotle and St Augustine are called to comment in The Good Body - Aristotle who considered thinness evidence of ‘rightly ordered desires’. And ordering, managing, controlling as necessary psychological mechanisms for those in the grip of the disorders arise again and again in both these bodies of work: the need to create order in the face of unmanageable emotional chaos, to preserve and conserve one area of personal territory untouchable by any other. As the anorexic narrator in the novel Life Size says: ‘anyone looking at me would know instantly that I was an artist: my medium myself, my materials air and bone and will … I thought the body could be redesigned as a perfect, self-sufficient machine. But the more I denied it, the louder it cried’ (Shute 1992); and Parker, a character in a story by Flannery O'Connor, one of the subjects under discussion in The Good Body, creates himself: ‘For Parker, as perhaps for other obsessive “body sculptors”, remodelling his body has been a mode not of cultural conformity, but of self absorption and control’ (p. 185).

Robert Royston

Robert Royston

LCP, London

Robert Royston  

Coming from a totally different direction to psychodynamic psychology and psychoanalysis, John Birtchnell offers a new theory of relating. His approach and way of thinking are made startlingly clear from the start. Newton, he writes, did not discover gravity, which was always there; he simply drew attention to it, pointing out that there is a pull between the earth and the falling apple. So he, Dr Birtchnell, approaches another universal phenomenon, relating; in a similar manner, he draws attention to a previously unattended phenomenon and introduces a new theory to explain its laws.

So we have, out there, an entity, a fact of nature if you like, and, over here, an observer who notices it, suddenly becomes curious and then begins to observe and construct a theory about the abstract and universal laws that govern it. Relating becomes a thing. He talks about situations in which there is a scarcity of relating. Relating is in short supply. In this cognitive vocabulary relating is not the outcome of the individual will operating with a personal purpose, but is a substance like food.

This approach leads to passages where one feels that what is being described is obvious but also, curiously, that the description is not entirely human. ‘One person has the capacity to give a particular state of relatedness to another or take a state of relatedness away from her/him. A person may choose to be friends with another or may chose to break off that friendship. Equally, a person may have a state of relationship given to her/him or taken away from her/him. In this sense, states of relatedness are like commodities that may be passed around, exchanged, bargained for, or fought over.’

As background to the new theory, Dr Birtchnell states that human behaviour is on a continuum with the behaviour of plants and animals. Relating to others, as one form of behaviour, is governed by the same physical laws that cause behaviour in plants and animals. Humans, however, differ from plants and insects in that our relating is accompanied by affect. This is a refinement with which we have been endowed through the course of evolution to reinforce advantageous forms of behaviour. So a pleasant emotion is a reward, and unpleasant emotion a punishment.

Response to M. and M. Rustin on Julius Caesar

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

9 Kestrel Close, Ewshot, Farnham, Surrey GU10 5TW

Meg Williams  

The problem which confronts us via the seductiveness of a Shakespeare play is, how can we let the meaning of the experience get through to us? How can we appreciate the living play, not colonize it with our own values, in fact, expand our experience? And in any attempt at literary criticism, the danger lies in failing to decipher the aesthetic structure of the drama, which is where the deep meaning resides. We don't need Shakespeare to tell us that politicians tell lies, or that murder doesn't work; we certainly don't need to pat him on the back for doing so. We do need Shakespeare, however, to express our emotions for us and to symbolize them into the form of a thinking process. This is an abstract function and is why the events of a poetic drama cannot be translated literally: the meaning of a ‘death’ derives from its poetic context; the representation of a commonsense ‘catastrophe’ (sudden violence) is not necessarily Bion's ‘catastrophic change’. Bion's concept describes that great achievement, a stage in the structural development of the mind; it is not something nasty that happened on the way to the forum. The real interest to psychoanalysis lies in the emotionally charged deep meaning, and the problem is, how to allow that meaning to work on us.

How then does Julius Caesar, this ‘play of fire and love’ (as Wilson Knight called it) shape our reactions? How are our sympathies guided, how can we gauge emotional temperature, indeed, what sort of place is Shakespeare's Rome? Certainly not Gorbachev's Russia with its suffering people and beleaguered leader. An analogy which corresponds with the dramatic tone of the play would be the great English public school; Julius Caesar is as much about the relationships and ideologies which came to be embodied in that institution as its sister-play, Henry V, is about English nationalism. There are various references to school and school-bonds (Casca was ‘quick mettle when he went to school’; Brutus and Volumnius were at school together); rivalry is keen and there is a strong sense of age-ranking with due deference paid to minor differences of perhaps a year or two - Julius and Cassius the eldest, Cassius an ‘elder soldier’ than Brutus, Antony younger than both, then Octavius and finally Lucius the boy under Brutus's protection. In the plebeians we have the playground hordes, ready to rehearse Hearts of Oak or Lord of the Flies - to tease the prefects (tribunes) or lynch the swots for their ‘bad verses’ (Cinna the Poet). These demand, above all, entertainment from the ‘Roman actors’ of the upper school (as Brutus terms them): references are rife to stage-play and acting, to earning one's place in the public eye. The tribunes who would ridicule Caesar's image (pull scarves off his statue) are ‘put to silence’. Caesar (head boy, cricket captain?)

responseSet.title: Reply to Langs and Badalamenti
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Reply to Langs and Badalamenti

Bernard Burgoyne

Bernard Burgoyne

Middlesex EN3 4SF

Bernard Burgoyne  

The work that Langs and Badalamenti (1994a) are engaged on is of great importance for the field of psychotherapy generally, and for the theory of communication in particular. I have said this repeatedly, both in public seminars, and in writing: I said it in the response that they comment on (Burgoyne 1994). What continually vitiates the claims that they put forward for their work is a certain lack of focus about the differences that exist between psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, and such imprecisions - many of which concern the problems of the nature of science - continue in their latest response (Langs & Badalamenti 1994b). I will try to address some of their comments.

The authors say that I claim that their research ‘is not at all related to psychoanalysis’. What I claimed is that their own theory and psychoanalysis are two competing programmes, each proposing itself as a science of communication or miscommunication; and I said that these programmes are clearly related. I stressed in particular the psychoanalytical roots of Langs's variables. I chose to mention his own description of his introduction of the idea of a Communication-scope: he proposed this innovation as a replacement for what he calls the older ‘Freud-scope’, both instruments aiming to study what in psychoanalysis is called unconscious structure. To say that their work is no longer work on psychoanalysis, which I do say, and to claim that their work has no relation to psychoanalysis are clearly two quite different criticisms.

The claims that they make about the unconscious depend, not surprisingly, on the theories that they hold about the unconscious, and also on the hypotheses that they ascribe to Freud's theory of the unconscious: they seem unaware of this. Furthermore, what it means to ‘validate’ a ‘measure of unconscious communication’ is additionally dependent on one's theory of the function of validation in the processes of science; a parallel caveat could be proposed about their assumption of the unproblematic nature of the term ‘empirical’. The authors tend to assume that these issues are straightforward, and finally answered by their work, instead of their being major and central problems located at the heart of any research problems in this area. Certainly these immense and far-ranging problems of methodology are unlikely to be resolved in forthcoming decades. When any scientist ‘goes to nature’, using the mathematical structures and formalisms that have been built into the scientific enterprise since the Renaissance, it is never ‘to allow nature to speak for itself, but to engage in a discourse with nature mediated by batteries of variables and assumptions.

Treating Survivors of Satanist Abuse edited by Valerie Sinason. Published by Routledge, London, 1994; 320 pages; £18.95.

David Black

David Black

London

David Black  

Satanism has traditionally been the inverse of Christianity. If Christianity condemns sexual promiscuity, Satanism is for it. If Christianity condemns buggery, Satanism is for it. If Christianity recites the Our Father forwards, Satanism recites it backwards. If in the Christian Mass the Eucharistic bread is white and circular, in the Black Mass it's black and triangular.

There is an element here of the playful rituals of many societies, such as the Roman Saturnalia or the medieval Lord of Misrule, in which for a short period the normal hierarchy of society is stood on its head. The initial attraction of Satanism is probably the intoxicating release of the repressed it appears to represent. Valerie Sinason suggests interestingly that many of today's Satanists are from fundamentalist religious backgrounds and, of course, Satanism is itself a fundamentalism: it does what in analytic language is called concrete thinking.

Once the first excitement is passed, Satanism turns into a relentless litany of compulsions, often of extraordinary viciousness. The need to avoid remorse (highly valued by Christians as by Kleinians) leads to extravagantly disgusting and cruel acts: one survivor, quoted here, describes how as a little girl she was hung up naked for two days ina sack full of creepie-crawlies; cult-members would periodically walk past and hit the sack, or poke things into it. ‘Typically,’ writes Mary Sue Moore,

children have hands and feet tied, may be gagged, are forced to watch dismemberment and beheadings of live animals, forced to eat or drink faeces or urine, often drugged and told they have had instruments ‘inserted into their body’ by surgery while drugged, are forced to watch or take part in the sexual and physical abuse of other children; often they are told by the robed or costumed adult perpetrators that they can be heard and observed by ‘Satan’ or the perpetrators anytime, anywhere, and that any attempt to tell outsiders will result in the torture and death of family members or themselves. (p. 231)

Carol Holmes

Carol Holmes

London

Carol Holmes  

Psychoanalysis and psychotherapy have generally tended to focus on the intrapsychic and distorted aspects of the patient's relationship with past early important figures. Robert Langs's development of the communicative approach to psychoanalytic psychotherapy, in contrast, acknowledges as one of the critical factors of the therapeutic relationship the patient's valid unconscious perceptions of important others. The approach is therefore concerned with the influence on the patient of the harmful inputs of the therapist.

[[RunningHead]]

Mental Space by Robert Young. Published by Process Press, London, 1994; 200 pages; £ 15.95.

Sara Cooper

Sara Cooper

London

Sara Cooper  

Dr Young sets out to do two things. Firstly, to locate psychoanalysis within ‘the history of thought about nature and human nature, with particular reference to Cartesian mind-body dualism’, and secondly, to address the question of ‘what enhances and constricts mental space’ in the light of different psychoanalytic approaches. These he categorizes according to whether they are ‘useful and resonant with our experience, as contrasted with scientific versions of psychology’.

The attempt to place psychoanalysis in an historical, social and cultural context is timely and one insufficiently considered by a rather solipsistic profession concerned with the inner world. Dr Young displays formidable erudition and encyclopaedic knowledge and bombards the reader with fascinating quotations. Indeed, the bibliography runs to 18 pages, including 46 references to the author's own papers, 20 to those of Freud, and 12 to Klein.

The book raises important issues about reification and concretization, problems which inevitably arise when any effort is made to define ‘mental space’. It explores interpretations and misinterpretations of reality within and without the analytic frame, particularly with reference to racism, one of the most destructive attributes of human beings. Indeed, the detailed exposition of the intertwining social and psychological components of racism seems to stand on its own as a study.

Dr Young provides a useful discussion of various psychoanalytic concepts, particularly of ones stemming from the object relations school, including projective identification and transitional space. He describes the former as ‘the most fruitful psychoanalytic concept since the discovery of the unconscious’ and as the one that ‘offers the key to understanding how the primitive integrates with the social’. He emphasizes the reductive, scientistic nature of the Freudian metaphors of forces and drives, preferring the Kleinian system on the grounds that it lays less claim to scientific certitude. He acknowledges that the term ‘object relations’ itself poses problems of reification, but suggests that the theory's emphasis on relationships between people, rather than on internal drives, resonates more closely with our experiences. He believes that the Kleinian model, which takes psychotic anxieties rather than the incest taboo as the nodal point for our defensive systems, offers greater potential for social change, since if we can recognize the normal and fundamental nature of our misinterpretations of reality, re-evaluation becomes possible.

Dear Book Reviews Editor

David Smith, in his latest correspondence in our ‘Grunbaum debate’, observes that he and I ‘are both concerned with the philosophical underpinnings of psychoanalysis and the intellectual status of psychoanalytic claims about mental life’ (British Journal of Psychotherapy 11(3): 491-3). I might address the philosophical (specifically, hermeneutic-phenomenological) issues another time.

Mourning Becomes …

Ian Craib

Ian Craib

Ian Craib  

Dear Editor

I am sorry that David Malan found my piece on mourning paranoid, contemptuous and extreme (British Journal of Psychotherapy 11(3)). However I do wish that despite such strong reactions he could have read it more carefully, and I wonder if I could take up a little more of your space to correct a couple of misrepresentations and reply to a couple of other points.

Firstly, Malan says'… he accuses Abraham, who merely pointed out that internalisation of the loved one was part of normal mourning, of trying to “establish the mourning process as an area of professional expertise and control”. Freud, Abraham and Klein “illustrate a process of a profession carving out an area of power for itself”…’

If he returns to these passages he will see that I say that the three theorists can be read in such a way but I spend the next page and a half trying to show how once Freud sets up the normal/pathological distinction it is undermined by Abraham, and even more by Klein, who, I say, is the ‘theorist who least fits into my argument’ and who shows the complexity of the mourning process.

Secondly, David Malan says that ‘If he spelled out more clearly that he is concerned with a trend in certain areas of society and psychotherapy, the article would be much more acceptable.’

More on Mourning

Andrew Samuels

Andrew Samuels

Andrew Samuels  

Dear Editor

I doubt I will be the only one to observe that David Malan's response to Ian Craib's paper does not remotely engage with its challenging theses (British Journal of Psychotherapy 11(3)).

As I understand it, Craib is calling for a degree of collective self-reflexivity and professional self-consciousness on the part of mental health professionals, especially psychoanalysts, psychoanalytic psychotherapists and group analytic psychotherapists.

He wants us to accept (a) that our ideas and practices cannot be sequestered from their relations with wider social, cultural and political forces; (b) that there is a degree of imperialism and self-benefit in the extension of therapy expertise into psychosocial areas such as dying, death and mourning (I see no judgementalism on Craib's part about this - the problems start when his point upsets people and so gets denied); (c) psychotherapy cannot avoid making a whole set of normalistic and moralistic statements about the phenomena it deals with. This mourning process is going well, that one pathologically, that one has only just started. Again, I don't read Craib as saying this is a terribly bad thing that we must stop doing, only that something of value in earlier theoretical formulations that valorized unpleasure may be being lost in a kind of feel-good manoeuvre that wins votes or clients in the short-term but evacuates depth in many other ways. In my opinion Dr Malan is, in a sense, caught up in a turf war over the psyche when he uses words like ‘paranoid’ to summarize the tone of a thoughtful and scholarly article.

To the extent that our field is in a state of (dis)ease, it has to seek some of the therapy it needs from the kinds of self-questioning theses and texts that are presently being produced by writers like Ian Craib who are well-versed in social theory. This means challenging the silly clinic-academy divide that has sprung up in which clinicians ‘feel’ and have the last word about ‘people’, and academics ‘think’ and have the last word about ‘ideas’.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Bion once said that feelings are one of the few things which analysts have the luxury of being able to regard as facts. Yet in this important area there is a theoretical gap. Psychoanalysis has often been criticized for not having worked out a theory of affect and it is true that there is no systematic examination of emotional states in the literature, nor a useful description of the psychology of emotional arousal. As we know, Freud approached the question of affect by beginning with the notion of pleasure and unpleasure. Freud described emotions as derivatives of instincts, as quantities of energy that disturb homeostatic equilibrium and which, unless they are discharged, are transformed into anxiety. Now, in modern British psychoanalysis and object relations theory, we no longer tend to take the view that emotions are tensions that need to be discharged, but more that they are states of mind that wax and wane within relationships and that emotions must be accepted and lived with. Far from getting in the way, as Freud thought, feeling states constantly accompany us, intrinsically interesting and enriching in themselves, a guide to our actions and something we like to share with others. In fact, we believe that the trouble really begins when we try to get rid of feelings. What moves us, touches us or gives us anxiety or pain is what we need to think about and try to understand. This activity constitutes symbol formation, assigns structure in the unconscious and orientates us within a stable and reliable psychic world. In thinking about feeling, we bring order to the turmoil that is so often the inheritance of childhood and the flux that accompanies us through life.

The British Journal of Psychotherapy and the Freud Museum co-sponsored a conference entitled ‘How do we think about feelings?’ last spring in which Andre Green presented a paper which contributes to the theoretical gap in affect theory. His ideas are rooted in a Freudian framework but he has strong reservations about the importance of infant research in furthering psychoanalytic argument. He proposes four types of emotional experience - tonality, feelings, emotions and passions - and describes their power to infuse and spread, to invade and overwhelm. They affect fantasy and all mental representations, and Green outlines the relationship of affect to these psychic structures and to consciousness and unconsciousness. Three more papers that elaborate how affect and idea combine to create meaning in clinical work were presented at the conference by Rosine Perelberg, Luis Rodriguez de la Sierra and Eric Rayner. The conference was chaired by David Bell whose commentary on the Green and Perelberg papers is included here.

[[RunningHead]]

How to Do Groups (Second Edition) by William Friedman. Published by Jason Aronson Inc., New Jersey, 1994; 274 pages; $30.00.

Michael Sevitt

Michael Sevitt

Epsom

Michael Sevitt  

I did not think that I would like this book. After all, it is American, which so often means jargon filled, and it's yet another in the How To Do … category. The notion that one can learn how to practise any variety of psychotherapy from reading a book has always struck me as fanciful. Yet my experience of reading this work has been salutary. Friedman has written an extremely accessible book which addresses many aspects of the group therapeutic encounter that assume importance to practitioners, yet are rarely written about. In the preface, he refers to the book as a road map, and he has a particular interest in offering practical guidelines to therapists working with groups for the first time.

In Chapter 1, ‘The first steps’, he assumes, interestingly, that a beginning group therapist will co-conduct her/his first group with a cotherapist and provides some sensible, uncontentious advice about choosing one. The subsequent section on models of supervision was less straightforward. Friedman's view is that the best form of supervision occurs when the supervisor is the cotherapist, principally because it provides a unique opportunity for a trainee to observe an experienced therapist in action. It would have been more helpful if he had made a clear distinction between learning through observation of an experienced therapist (a valuable learning experience for a trainee) and supervision proper. However, he makes valuable points about the limitations of supervision via verbal report, though his dismissal of what is the most widely practised model as one to be avoided wherever possible, seems pretty sweeping.

The next two chapters focus on referral, selection and screening of patients. Friedman covers a wide range of practical issues, concentrating especially on those tensions arising from the differential status between individual and group therapy, and those involved in deciding whether to start a group as soon as possible for fear of losing patients or to delay until a group of sufficient size has been put together. I was disappointed that he has little to say about the composition of a group and especially the need to consider carefully whether to include an isolate, i.e. someone who differs from all the other members along one important dimension and who may therefore subsequently become a vehicle for their projections. Neither does he discuss the different implications of closed, fixed-term versus slow-open groups.

Barry Palmer

Barry Palmer

London

Barry Palmer  

This is an important book. The authors put forward what they claim to be a new paradigm for understanding the individual and the group: ‘The individual and the group have overtime become reified entities, ‘things’ compartmentalized into separate areas of investigation, thereby disguising the underlying unity of the processes of human interaction’ (p. 12). Their project is to construct a theory integrating current theories of individual personality and group dynamics. They suggest that the work of Freud, Bion and others already hints at their essential unity. What makes a more thoroughgoing synthesis possible now is the advent of systems theory, and of a theory of knowing which is transforming the natural and human sciences.

The book is in four parts. In the first part, the writers outline their new paradigm based on three premises. Firstly, that ‘inner and group life are linked by a communication system of verbal and non-verbal interactions linking members of a group’ (p. 13). So:

… the paradigm linking psychoanalysis and group dynamics calls for observation of … three or more systems or processes: the internal or intrapsychic system of the persons in the group; the system of communications and ‘acts’ among two or more persons; and the group-qua-group. (pp. 14f)

Secondly, that ‘the individual and the group emerge from a primal unity through the creation of a boundary which distinguishes one from the other’ (p. 17). Thirdly, that ‘the principle of complementarity accounts for the multidimensional nature of group relations’ (p. 20).

Sylvia Hutchinson

Sylvia Hutchinson

London

Sylvia Hutchinson  

This weighty volume has as its primary focus the empirical basis of group psychotherapy. It is an impressive and scholarly work that should prove an invaluable resource and guide to researchers in the field. The book aims to provide a comprehensive review of those theoretical and clinical issues that are grounded in a substantial body of empirical literature, and challenges a ‘conceptual’ literature (representing by far the majority of published articles) that pays no heed to, and fails to integrate, empirical data. The status of this volume is greatly enhanced by including amongst its contributors some of the leading figures in group psychotherapy research.

The book is organized into four parts: conceptual and methodological foundations; structural entities in group psychotherapy; therapeutic components of the group ecosystem; and special applications and populations. In Part 1 the editors track the multiple origins and historical roots of group psychotherapy, providing an evolutionary map to locate the emergence of major research themes. The startling paucity of reference to developments in group psychotherapy in Europe is sobering and is a likely reflection of the relative lack of research reporting outside America. An overview of outcome research to date confirms the efficacy of group treatment and shows an increasing experimental rigour in research design and analysis. This is, however, accompanied by disconcerting, recent trends that indicate a raised profile for cognitive/behavioural (a model which does not particularly harness group-specific factors) research data with specific client populations, and a diminishing focus on interpersonal models and on the group as a dynamic/therapeutic entity. Chapter 2 provides a guide to methodological issues and a very handy flowchart mapping out design and analysis considerations for the researcher. The editors manage to enliven their painstaking and thorough evaluative review with a keen sense of the complexity of the field and an honest and uncompromising commitment to its development. They and other contributors urge greater elaboration and articulation of conceptual models and definitions, repeated use of the same measuring instruments to increase the generalizability of results, and increased collaboration between researchers and practitioners.

Jenny Duckham  

There has long been a gap in the International Library of Group Psychotherapy and Group Process of publications addressing extensively the subject of supervision. For any reader wishing to be acquainted with the training of group-analytic psychotherapists using the tripartite structure of personal therapy, theoretical seminars and supervision of practice, all pursued in the group setting, as experienced and practised by graduates of the London Institute of Group Analysis (IGA), then this is the book to buy.

Meg Sharpe was one of the first graduates of the IGA and for many years has been a well-respected training analyst and supervisor. This, together with a period as Chair of the Training Committee and experience of teaching the model to students abroad, especially in Norway, has given her a broad perspective and critical awareness of the many issues raised in supervision. In this book she has brought together a wealth of knowledge and reflection, theory and practice, questions and answers, and much more, by using lively contributions from teaching staff, practitioners and students.

Ronald Baker

Ronald Baker

London

Ronald Baker  

This is an interesting and useful book which delivers precisely what it proposes, the delineation of the purpose and meaning of jokes from a psychoanalytic perspective. It is written with clarity and style. It is both an easy and a serious read, lovingly composed by an author with a life-long preoccupation with jokes and humour. The

267

text includes over 300 jokes and humorous anecdotes from a wide range of situations. Like all such collections, it contains some brilliant examples but suffers from the perennial problem that a joke that is read rarely carries the impact that it does when told.

Dr Strean departs strikingly from the position taken by many authors who attempt a scholarly work on this subject in that he shares intimate and personal details of his own life in the service of making some of the jokes more understandable. This is a courageous and spirited stance which effectively underlines the view that jokes are an important and revealing communication when made by a patient in psychotherapy or analysis.

Strean recognizes that the problem-ridden issues that inevitably reach the ears of a psychotherapist are one and the same as those expressed in the jokes exchanged between individuals in everyday communications. The strength of the book is thus contained in his commitment as a psychotherapist to concern himself with the hopes, conflicts, fantasies, pain and anxieties that patients bring to the treatment setting, and to demonstrate to the reader how jokes can reflect just these areas of human turmoil. And he does this impressively.

The book is carefully structured. It begins with a chapter on the psychological components of jokes, their common properties, the manner in which unconscious fantasies, wishes and defences are expressed in them and the way in which super-ego injunctions are broken by the teller and his listener(s). This unfolds with clarity and is both comprehensive and enlightening. It covers some of the ground traversed by Freud (1905) in ‘Jokes and their relation to the unconscious’, but it is more systematic and less complex which makes it accessible to readers not acquainted with psychoanalytic literature. Special emphasis is given to the diagnostic significance of a patient's favourite joke. The subsequent chapters deal with jokes on sex, marriage, parent-child relationships, religion, race and psychotherapists/psychoanalysts. In every case, Strean describes the psychological and unconscious components of a clinical situation in which a patient manifests conflict and pain in one of these areas in a manner reflecting compassion and understanding, only then proceeding to illustrate how the same situations occur in jokes and the unconscious reasons for this.

Sara Cooper

Sara Cooper

London

Sara Cooper  

According to the OED a handbook is ‘a small book … such as may be held in the hand’, and also ‘a book containing concise information for the tourist’. This handbook is neither particularly small nor handy since it attempts to cover a vast terrain. So, what kind of tourist has it in mind, the casual day-tripper wanting to know what psychotherapy is, or the serious traveller wanting to know more about the history and topography of this journey?

According to its blurb it is ‘for all health professionals and anyone interested in psychotherapy as practitioner, patient or general reader’. This is a remarkably wide brief: to introduce the non-professional to different types of psychotherapy and to some of its underlying issues and at the same time to be of interest to the practitioner. Surprisingly, there is something in it for both.

It is divided into five sections: Introduction, Culture, Modalities, Settings and Issues. The section entitled Culture, which includes race, gender, sexual orientation etc., raised some important questions, including the validity of having such a section. I wonder whether the ways in which such issues are addressed within a therapeutic context may depend more on the therapist's theoretical orientation than on their politics and value systems. This is particularly clear in Judith Hassan's fascinating contribution on working with survivors of the Nazi Holocaust. Her chapter was not, in fact, about culture but about her understanding of how to work with individuals who have been through this unique trauma, i.e. about theory and practice.

I found it interesting to compare this book with a previous handbook, Windy Dryden's Individual Therapy: A Handbook. Dryden gave an overview of different theoretical approaches, Freudian, Jungian, Rogerian, Cognitive etc., while the handbook under review summarizes theories in a chapter, with several references to Dryden's book amongst others, and attempts to take us a step further by addressing issues and, in particular, contexts for therapeutic work.

Abstracts from other Journals

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis76, 457, 1995

The Concept of ‘Early Triangulation’ as a Key to a Unified Model of Hysteria

Ute Rupprecht-Schampera

On the basis of a subtle and critical use of the concepts of separation and triangulation, this paper develops a psychodynamically unified model of the multi-faceted phenomenology of hysteria in both women and men. It offers an explanation for the manner in which preoedipal and oedipal factors interact in hysteria. The fundamental conflict in malignant and benign hysterias is assumed to have the same content, the severity of the disturbance being determined by qualitative and quantitative factors (specific relational constellations, specific forms of traumatization, and the subject's age, maturity and ability to cope with the relevant problems). The fundamental conflict common to all hysterias is deemed to lie in the subject's attempt to utilize oedipal triangulation in the context of a sexualized form of relationship with the parent of opposite sex, in order to obtain by force the missing early (preoedipal) triangulation (in the case of female hysterics) or to secure a substitute for it (in male hysterics), and thereby to achieve the separation from the mother that could not originally be negotiated. Traumatization and typical defensive constellations associated with this neurotic attempt at resolution are described. The same theoretical approach makes it possible to understand the interactional function of conversion symptoms, and at the same time to consider their significance for this specific neurotic configuration.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis76, 475, 1995

Countertransference: The Emerging Common Ground

Glen O. Gabbard

In the last decade or so, the understanding of countertransference has become an emerging area of common ground among psychoanalysts of diverse theoretical perspectives. This convergence can be traced to the development of two key concepts - projective identification and countertransference enactment. Projective identification has evolved from a patient's intrapsychic fantasy in Klein's original work to an interpersonal interaction between patient and analyst. The notion of countertransference enactment has been widely used to capture clinical situations in which a countertransference reaction in the analyst corresponds to the patient's attempt to actualize a transference fantasy. These ideas, in conjunction with the contributions of social constructivists and relational theorists, as well as Sandler's conceptualization of roleresponsiveness, have led to an understanding of countertransference as a ‘joint creation’ by analyst and patient. The relative contributions of analyst and patient vary somewhat according to the theoretical perspective espoused by the analyst. This common ground is best regarded as comprising a gradient or continuum in which more weight is given to the analyst's contribution on one end of the continuum and more emphasis to the patient's contribution on the other. While countertransference enactments are widely regarded as inevitable, their role in creating intrapsychic change is more controversial.

Discussion

Ann Scott: I'd like to thank both speakers very warmly. Could I start by asking Tony Ryle whether he would like to make any response to Peter Fonagy's paper?

Tony Ryle: I think honestly it'd be better if we let the assembled multitude bring up the points that they'd like.

Andrew Samuels: I'll get the ball rolling. While this was going on, I was having a fantasy - what Jungians call ‘active imagination’ when they're not writing about the self - and in it I was asking myself: how would the debate go if it was CAT that had started at the end of the last century, in an exotic locale in the middle of Europe, and what if Peter was the Ryle Professor of CAT now; and what would be said about psychoanalysis? Because the thrust of the whole thing seemed to me to be psychoanalysis looking at CAT, rather than the other way round. And I wonder what, if CAT were the senior therapy, CAT would say about psychoanalysis.

Tony Ryle: It requires a very radical rethink, because in fact it wasn't that way round, and intellectual history takes place, and one reads things and learns things from the last 100 years.

Member of the audience: Try and imagine ‥ .

Tony Ryle: I'm too pragmatic and down-to-earth for that!

Andrew Samuels: I have some ideas, but they may seem not very nice to psychoanalysis (then after all that can't be helped) [Laughter]. I wonder if CAT would see psychoanalysis as a therapy overly concerned with conformism or adaptation; invested in an adultomorphic fantasy about the child? Now these are picked up from Tony Ryle's talk. And I wonder if CAT would say that psychoanalysis perpetuates dependency on the basis of a power imbalance, or something like that? Would that be the kind of thing we could fantasise about?

Tony Ryle: Well, the other way round, I could ask some questions about whether the insights achieved through the regression induced by intensive and long-term treatment are necessarily the best or the only road to a radical change in the individual. Most learning takes place by complexification and accumulation, and not by stripping away. And I certainly would echo the bit about my worry about the power relationship between analyst and patient. It may be necessary in some cases, but I think in other cases it's been used in very destructive ways; and is still being used in ways that I feel are destructive. So in that sense you've picked up one or two fantasies that I'm prepared to echo for you.

The Importance of Disappointment by Ian Craib. Published by Routledge, London, 1994; 205 pages; £37.50 (hardback), £12.99 (paperback).

Neville Singh

Neville Singh

Neville Singh  

This book is a useful addition to the growing library of critical studies and surveys of the post-modern condition. The choice of subject-matter is timely because of our increasingly contradictory relationship with disappointment in all its forms. The Introduction states that ‘(this book) explores the nature of identity in late modern society’. Furthermore, that by retrieving and examining the ‘“negative” strands of psychoanalysis’, i.e. its articulation of meaningful - because realistic - disappointments, ‘psychoanalytic therapy can become more than ideology, (thus) offering genuine help to its patients and providing a real source of radical social criticism’.

The author is well placed to advance this particular critique for he is both a sociologist and a psychoanalytic group psychotherapist. His thesis is that ‘there is much about our modern world that increases disappointment and at the same time encourages us to hide from it’ (my italics). Psychoanalysis and its off-shoots are implicated in this predicament. The text is a relatively easy read and is impressively referenced. It is possible though that psychoanalysts might be surprised to read about ‘psychoanalysis … promising results that are competitive rather than realistic’. To my knowledge, psychoanalysts tend to be cautious and ever-mindful of the reality principle.

Dr Craib's main argument is with these aspects (belief systems) of psychoanalysis which continue to influence our understanding of and approach to the human condition in late modern society. They are, broadly speaking, reductionistic on the one hand and naively emancipative on the other, with each stance susceptible to ideological misguidedness and/or misuse. He supports his argument by way of succinct (if somewhat selective) critical overviews of well-known Freudian and Kleinian concepts as well as close readings of Bowlby and Winnicott and those within the British independent school of psychoanalysis. I noted the following interesting comment of Dr Craib's on the differing philosophical outlook of Freud and Klein on one hand, and that of Bowlby and Winnicott on the other. That is, whereas Freud and Klein focus on ‘how people are as messy and conflict-ridden and nasty as they are integrated, capable and nice’… ‘the work of Winnicott and Bowlby has been taken up to demonstrate how people should be …’. This is followed by Dr Craib-the-sociologist observing that ‘A programme of social engineering can be found in their (Freud's and Klein's) work, but it remains ambiguous; in the work of Winnicott and Bowlby it becomes much clearer’ (excerpts from the aptly titled Chapter 4: ‘Looking on the bright side’, p. 61). Similar sharp observations are embedded in the text.
