Crispin Lane

Crispin Lane

Lincoln Centre, London

Crispin Lane  

This collection of 30 ‘essential papers’ is divided into six sections, under the respective rubrics of Historical Papers, Drive Theory, Ego Psychology, Object Relations Theory, Self Psychology, and Issues and Techniques in Treatment. As an American publication, it is hardly surprising that the sections on the application of ego and self psychology take up half the book, and interesting to compare these perspectives with the more familiar orientation of British writers.

The historically-minded reader has here the opportunity of surveying the evolution of clinical attitudes to the addicted patient, as early ‘moral hygienic’ stances develop into something deeper and more complicated. The Freud papers do not deal directly with alcoholism per se, but rather with addiction generically (‘Masturbation as the Original Addiction’) and compulsive gambling (the Dostoievsky study). It is salutary to remember that Freud's addiction (to cigars) eventually killed him.

The psychopathology of addiction is particularly overdetermined, and these papers offer a wide range of approaches that in turn examine and emphasis different factors involved in the selection and maintenance of this way of life. As a result I sometimes felt that it suffers from the perhaps intrinsic drawback of anthologies, a sort of incoherent heterogeneity, but on the whole the impression is of a useful inclusiveness that allows the reader to think around the central issues and examine them from a multiplicity of viewpoints. Early polemical papers on the status of alcoholism as a disease, an approach which can help the patient to begin to come to terms with his guilt and which insists on the need for sobriety if progress is to be achieved (Jellinek is of this type) are complemented by those dealing with the syndrome as a symptom so that the underlying conflicts can be addressed. This ‘bifocal’ or ‘binocular’ consideration is implicit throughout.

On Flirtation by Adam Phillips. Published by Faber, London and Boston, 1994; 226 pages; £14.99.

Charles Rycroft

Charles Rycroft

London

Charles Rycroft  

One of the present reviewer's recurrent whimsies has long been the idea that one day, when psychoanalysis has been forgotten by medicine and psychiatry, it will be found still to be alive and well in the English departments of, particularly, American universities. On Flirtation had me momentarily fearing that this might prove to be something more than a mere fancy.

The author, Adam Phillips, is indeed a literary critic turned psychotherapist, and his way of thinking, his style of writing, remains militantly ‘literary’, in both the good and bad senses of that word. If he were an architect, his buildings would be baroque, with fascinating, exuberant detail obscuring appreciation of their basic structure. He uses adjectives, adverbs and subordinate clauses not, as a ‘scientific’ writer would, to specify his meaning more precisely, but to allude to issues remote from what he is talking about; the effect is both scintillating and distracting.

I must give some examples. When Phillips writes ‘It was part of Freud's disingenuous rationalism to assert …,’ he momentarily induces the distracting thought ‘so Phillips thinks Freud's rationalism was not just naive but insincere’. When he writes ‘Kristeva writes with beguiling confidence “analytic cure can implement a genuine graft of symbolic potential”’, one is diverted from elucidating Kristeva's meaning - how are grafts of potential implemented? - by having to wonder why Kristeva's statement is noteworthily confident, and why her confidence is beguiling. And when he writes ‘and even Lacan found Hamlet reassuring’, whatever does that ‘even’ mean?

In defence of Phillips's style, it must be said that all the essays reprinted in On Flirtation were written for literary audiences, most of them being book reviews contributed to The London Review of Books, where verbal firework displays are entirely acceptable. There is nonetheless an overarching theme, accurately even if whimsically defined by his title.

Phillips is against ‘commitment’, on the grounds that it leads to dogmatism as opposed to healthy scepticism; to self-righteous earnestness as opposed to joyous playfulness, and to reluctance to explore aspects of one's personality which one has not included in one's self-image. So, to avoid the perils and restrictions of commitment, one should flirt with ideas, flirt with others and with one's own various unexplored selves.

The Dream of Psychoanalysis: Irma's Dream, Some Commentaries, and a Contemplation of its Navel

Sian Morgan

Sian Morgan

26 Newnham Road, Cambridge

Sian Morgan  

Freud's dream of 1895, ‘Irma's Dream’, stands at the beginning of psychoanalytic theory, but Freud's analysis only glancingly refers to the ‘unknown’ elements that are found at ‘the navel of the dream’. The imagery of the dream suggests this phrasing is significant and that unconscious elements refer to the oracle at Delphi. At Delphi a chthonic goddess was supplanted by a patriarchy; the ‘unknown’ at the centre of the dream is the archaic mother, repressed by Freud and by the patriarchal character of early psychoanalytic theory.

Joscelyn Richards

Joscelyn Richards

Willesden Hospital
Harlesden Road
London NW1O 3RY

Joscelyn Richards  

In this paper narcoleptic states refer to states of drowsiness or sleep that occur both within the patient and the psychotherapist during a psychoanalytic psychotherapy session. The meaning is explored of recurring narcolepsy in a female patient for a period of four and a half years during her psychotherapy. The concept of internal cohabitation, which is a development of Bion's concepts of psychotic and non-psychotic personalities, is used to understand the narcoleptic phenomena in both patient and therapist and to explain the changes that took place in the patient.

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner  

This paper aims to explore aspects of psychoanalytic psychotherapy training, with particular reference to the pressures and uncertainties experienced following graduation. The prestige of the professional position places expectations ‘to know’, so there is an ambivalence in remaining open to analytic knowledge as supposition. The effect of unconscious processes is examined alongside the influence of role responsiveness. The concept of ‘embodied knowledge’ is proposed as a possible synthesis of the experiential and learning processes, whilst still leaving us with an open rather than restricted perspective.

[[RunningHead]]

Response to ‘Defensive Organizations or Collusive Interpretations?’ by Anthony Ryle

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Meira Likierman  

This is the third paper in which Ryle challenges the Kleinian view of defensive organizations in the borderline personality, the first two having addressed the works of Steiner and Joseph. Ryle states that his aim is ‘to challenge the ideas and orthodoxies’ which the three papers represent, and not ‘to attack the particular protagonists who have been prepared to offer their work for examination’.

Fair enough, except that I would firstly question the possibility of such a neat division in psychoanalytic debate. It is not easy to challenge the abstract content of a paper without in some way implicating the artistry that is revealed in the practice. Because clinical papers are particular examples of artistry, they may not offer fixed prescriptions that transfer readily from one clinical situation to another. Rather, they are partly valuable for their evocative power and our ability, through issues that they illuminate, to glimpse new clinical possibilities.

This does not preclude a rigorous examination of the author's framework. However, it is, by now, broadly accepted that patients improve with practitioners who hold different theoretical frameworks. This suggests that ‘either’ ‘or’ outlooks that emphasize only the virtues of one theoretical system at the expense of another might be missing the point.

It is with such thoughts in mind that I wish to respond more particularly to Ryle's criticism. Ryle's aim of ‘joint work’ with the patient that seeks to offer ‘an experience of a thoughtful collaborative relationship’ is no doubt one that O'Shaughnessy would applaud. The difficulty lies in the degree of anxiety and illness which made it impossible for her patient to engage in such a relationship for many years.

Generally speaking, the borderline patient might well be struggling unsuccessfully to connect self states across shifts within the session, and could in this sense legitimately be described as trying out restricted and unsatisfactory modes of relating in the transference. However, O'Shaughnessy's paper addresses the point that such restricted modes of relating are typically precarious, and in the absence of support, are liable to breakdown. The terror and suffering to which this can expose a borderline individual are captured more fully for me in the concept of a weak ego. By comparison terms such as ‘self state’, ‘role’ and ‘repertoire’ suggest a more advanced psychic situation in which the individual has some mastery over organizing his or her object relations.

Essentials of Psychoanalysis by Herbert Strean. Published by Brunner/Mazel, New York, 1994; 162 pages; £14.95.

An Introduction to the Therapeutic Frame by Anne Gray. Published by Routledge, London 1994; 162 pages; £12.95.

Sue Gerhardt

Sue Gerhardt

Oxford

Sue Gerhardt  

Herbert Strean sets out to provide a book to explain to psychiatrists, social workers and psychologists how to incorporate an understanding of unconscious processes into their work. He claims to offer ‘a clear introductory summary’ of psychoanalysis. Unfortunately, his summaries have the compressed clarity only of lecture notes. He makes little attempt to explain or persuade. For example, I cannot imagine a social worker being able to make any use of his one sentence descriptions of condensation, displacement and symbolization in primary process thinking. He does not relate such ideas to practice in a digestible way. Patrick Casement's discussion of unconscious symmetry in primary process thinking (in On Learning from the Patient) brings the topic to life in a way that this book does not. Whilst reading it, I had a recurring image of Herbert Strean looking through his lecture notes and speaking into a dictating machine. His tone is complacent and overfamiliar, yet curiously lacking in any intellectual context.

This lack of context is evident also in his failure to make clear that he is writing as an orthodox Freudian. For him, psychoanalysis is about discharging instinctual wishes and dealing with intrapsychic conflict; wishes are sexual wishes, anxiety is suppressed sexual excitement, and hysteria is the result of incestuous oedipal wishes. This approach is given as the ‘norm’, whilst later thinkers are presented as optional extras to be added on.

He makes no attempt to integrate other theories nor to discuss their merits. The ‘major concepts’ of Jung, Adler, Rank, Homey, Sullivan, Reich, Hartmann, Anna Freud, Erikson, Klein, Winnicott and Kohut are summarized in a few lines each. This whirlwind tour of psychoanalytic writing does not enable the reader to think. It seems to work more as a sort of Who's Who in psychoanalysis, enabling the reader to claim to have at least ‘heard of’ so and so.

The section on Klein is particularly weak. He claims that Klein thought that ‘part of development in the first and second years of life is an inevitable depression when the youngster feels separate from the mother; and that a little later the child finds himself or herself in the “paranoid-schizoid” position’. This is plain wrong.

Anyone who has seen Wim Wenders's great film, Wings of Desire, will recall how it is punctuated by the voices of children asking the sort of awkward questions that children ask like ‘Why am I me and not you?’, ‘Why am I here and not there?’, ‘When did time begin and where does space end?’. Problems with Transference Interpretations in Short-Term Dynamic Therapy

Mark Pearson

Mark Pearson

Queensbridge Road, Birmingham B13 8QD

Mark Pearson  

In this paper, I examine some problems which have arisen when I have attempted to make transference interpretations during short-term individual and group psychodynamic psychotherapy, and suggest an alternative style of working, which involves monitoring the transference but making comments using the material which the patient brings to the therapy session. This material is often not about the therapist-patient relationship, and I will argue that patients will frequently prefer to work in other areas for reasons of space and safety. For the therapist, the dangers of becoming intrusive and driving the patient into an impasse often outweigh the advantages of the directness that comes from examining the here and now relationship. I call this alternative style of working, ‘staying within the patient's metaphor’.

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

ACP, London

Anne Alvarez  

This beautifully composed and lucid book sets out to re-examine the two myths on which much of early psychoanalytic theory is based, and then to show us what we can now understand is missing, both within the interpretations of the myths themselves, and outside, in the transitional areas of experience which Hamilton suggests lie between them and span them. The author herself was trained as a Child and Adult Psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic in Britain, but has worked about half of her professional life as a psychotherapist and lecturer in the USA. What many people trained in the British Object Relations tradition would regard as theory of early and rather historical interest is still current in the United States. She shows, however, that these issues are not simply of historical interest here; her intellectual rigour and nose for sniffing out the meta-theory which lies behind the theory (she has a training in philosophy) show us how regularly some of these early ‘mistakes’ continue to invade our thinking. ‘Mistake’ is my word and probably a bad one, for Hamilton is interested in the nature of knowledge, and especially in its incompleteness, rather than its incorrectness. She examines the psychoanalytic tragic vision of knowledge from this point of view. She is sensitive to literature and is delicately attuned to the developmental potential of her patients, so the clinical and literary sections make beautiful and easy reading.

[[RunningHead]]

A Parallel Development

Francis Grier

Francis Grier

65 Tynemouth Road, London N15 4AU

Francis Grier  

From the first, I was struck by the contradictory feelings engendered in me by Michael. There seemed to be two main pairs of contrasts: one between his utterly affectless, non-communicative tone of voice and the seething content of his words; and another between his apparent attitude of hostile indifference to me (which was soon reciprocated) and my paradoxical realisation that there was yet something I found very likeable about him. He was a tall, handsome man of about 40 who, despite his apparently relaxed demeanour and dress, struck me as forged out of steel. It clearly irked him to find himself in counselling at all, but he had referred himself because of a depressed feeling that there was no point in living, no reason to get out of bed in the morning to face yet another boring day. He was clearly bored and irritated at having to tell his story yet again, which he proceeded to do although I had not asked him to. He told me of how he was the eldest of five children, born in Taiwan to an English mother and a half-German, half-Czech father of German nationality. The next child had arrived when he was two, and at three his parents decided to leave for Brazil. His father went there immediately and his mother took her, by then, three children to England where she parked them off in some kind of hostel - Michael was not clear about the details, but he is sure it was not a relative's home - whilst she went to join her husband. The children were flown over to join their parents about six months later. Michael's memories of this period consisted not of any sad or angry feelings but of being ‘the big brother’, looking after his two younger sisters. After about three years in Brazil the family moved to Germany. Michael emphasised in passing that he had had a very happy relationship with both his parents throughout his childhood; he portrayed the mutual feelings between him and his mother as rosy, and as he informed me of his father's international athletic status I sensed that he had looked up to him as if to a god.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

As much as we might struggle to keep undiluted versions of psychoanalysis available to those who need it and can use it, its labour-intensive nature makes this desideratum ever more difficult. Psychoanalysis creates a special domain, set apart from ordinary life, in which infant experience comes into the foreground; the full-blown transference becomes, in Freud's words, ‘a playground in which it is allowed to expand in almost complete freedom and in which it is expected to display to us everything in the way of pathogenic instincts hidden in the patient's mind’ (1914, p. 154). The evolution of the concept of transference means that this special experience can be used to explore beyond infancy to what it means to relate altogether. For individuals suffering a paucity of human relationships or gross distortions in self and object experience, transference work offers potentialities for the enrichment of human intimacy that can bring about an improvement in mental health and crucial life changes quite possibly unobtainable elsewhere.

In this issue Mark Pearson offers a review of the transference literature, but argues that some patients find transference interpretation threatening or intrusive. He believes that transformation of core relationship problems can be wrought equally as much by ‘staying within the patient's metaphor’, advocating the narrative or storytelling approach that seems to be being incorporated into psychoanalytic theory more and more lately. In a critique of the concept of transference, Nick Handley discusses how it can be used inappropriately to protect the analyst, to deny the real aspects of the therapeutic relationship or to create iatrogenic problems. He resituates the theory of transference within the existential-phenomenological encounter, suggesting that this gives it a firmer footing in clinical reality.

The theme of transference wends its way, inevitably, through the other papers in this issue. Gertrud Mander offers an exploration of psychodynamic once-weekly work and relates her experiences in which containment and analysis in the transference of high levels of primitive emotion are possible. Robert Royston's article on intellectual dysfunction tracks its roots to the effects of a childhood ‘autocratic object’ that prevents taking in and metabolizing new material, discernible in the transference. What are the implications for the transference when touch plays a role in the therapy, as in the many body-orientated therapies presently in fashion? Viqui Rosenberg writes of moving with a patient from a bioenergetics framework into a psychoanalytic one, with the suggestion that the change from the sphere of body boundaries and tensions into a distanced verbal space fostered oedipal-level work and symbol formation.

The Concept of Transference: A Critique

Nick Handley

Nick Handley

Warrington WA2 8RR

Nick Handley  

In this paper, after noting the history of the development of the concept of transference and its application in clinical pratice, I offer a resume of some major criticisms of the concept. I pay special attention to a critique which may be made from an existential phenomenological perspective. I evaluate the current status of the concept of transference in clinical practice, arguing that the concept of transference should be retained, but placed on a sounder phenomenological footing, as advocated by authors such as May (1961, 1967), Boss (1963, 1979) and Binswanger (1962, 1963).

responseSet.title: Response to ‘Teaching Klein’ by Linda Buckingham
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Response to ‘Teaching Klein’ by Linda Buckingham

Juliet Miller

Juliet Miller

60 Grove Park Terrace, Chiswick, London W4 3QE

Juliet Miller  

I was very interested to read Linda Buckingham's paper ‘Teaching Klein’ (Buckingham 1994), as I recently completed a course in Psychodynamic Counselling at a training institution in London where a majority of the theoretical input was Kleinian. Buckingham's discussion of the problems raised on a Kleinian training appear familiar to me, and this response is not to disagree with any points she raised but rather to add something from the student's perspective.

Within a reasonably eclectic training, dispute about Klein and her theories was frequently an area of discussion between students, generating high levels of anxiety, anger and splits within groups. I eventually felt that these discussions reflected a far more fundamental disagreement about how we all wanted to think and work in the consultingroom rather than simply about the merits of, or difficulties with, Kleinian theory.

Buckingham suggests that Kleinian theories seem particularly difficult initially for students to swallow, and I would agree with her that this is true for some students. However, in my experience, it appeared that as we became more familiar with Klein's theories there were two distinct reactions to whether or not they were considered to be a helpful tool in the clinical work.

Positive responses and a growing ability to play with and use her ideas came from those students who felt the need for reliable answers that they could use to inform them in the consulting-room. For these students the extensive body of Klein's work which deals so comprehensively with the internal world of the child became a map which they felt helped them to see their way through the confusing world of the consulting-room. So for some students Klein's strong faith in her own theories was a relief.

Negative and antagonistic reactions to Klein's theories seemed to come from those students who themselves felt uncomfortable with the possibility that there was one answer or one map, and who therefore felt claustrophobic and restricted within the apparent surefootedness of Kleinian theory rather than supported by it. These students seemed to be looking for ideas and theories which opened up the possibility of many ways of understanding where symbolism played more of a part. For them having one answer was not a relief but appeared to be a constraint.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

From Objects to Subjects

Susie Orbach and Luise Eichenbaum

Luise Eichenbaum

2 Lancaster Drive, London NW3 4HA

Luise Eichenbaum  

In the last few years gender-conscious workers in the field have shed light on the crisis in masculinity; they have deconstructed our fallacious notions of homosexuality, of heterosexuality and made the links between practices of exclusion and inclusion that marginalize not just women but vast sections of the population. A psychoanalytically informed feminism has been able to situate itself as social criticism. The interrogative scope of the gender-conscious psychoanalytic thinker has been enormous and has opened up important new ways for us to see and think about organizing the private and the public domain. Within psychoanalysis, a gender-conscious perspective has suggested important new ways of conceiving and working with women and men with a most important shift occurring in our understandings of feminine subjectivity. At its core, this shift has reshaped the view of woman as object, whether as analyst or analysand, to woman as subject.

A brief account of our own work across two continents traces this shift by looking at where we've been clinically, technically and theoretically. While our understandings have become elaborated over time, our initial observations, starting from our work in the early seventies in New York and then at The Women's Therapy Centre in London, continue to be useful.

The most striking feature of our work with women - and we are drawing now on the large pool of women from different class, age, cultural, sexual and political backgrounds and orientations - was the deep shame, resistance and confusion which coalesced around the issues of dependency, neediness and desire for attachment. Women we saw in therapy came with a variety of concerns ranging from obsessional symptomatology to feelings of depersonalization, a sense of fragmentation, an inability to express themselves, to know about their own desire apart from their response to the behaviour of others, inexplicable feelings of loss, emptiness or wariness, disturbing anger, a sense of doing for others but bereft of self-motivated agency. In other words, the emotional range seen by any psychotherapist in the course of their work. But, because we were involved in the project of theorizing about women's psychological development from a feminist perspective, the commonality of experience of our women patients had particular meaning for us.

[[RunningHead]]

History of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

167 Sumatra Road, London NW6 1PN

Michael Pokorny  

Many of you have said that you would like to have an outline of how we came to celebrate the launch of the National Register of Psychotherapists on 20 May 1993 in a ceremony at the House of Lords. Our story seems to begin in 1971 when the Foster Report recommended, as an aside, that the profession of psychotherapy should be regulated. Starting in 1975 the Joint Professions Working Party, chaired by the late Paul Sieghart, recommended in its 1978 Report that Indicative Registration was appropriate for psychotherapists. This meant that only registered practitioners would be legally allowed to call themselves psychotherapists. The Behavioural Psychotherapists wrote a dissenting appendix which denied the need for any kind of registration for psychotherapists.

In this atmosphere of shared mistrust a number of psychotherapy organisations went to a meeting at the Department of Health where they were told by the Minister that unless the profession could agree there was nothing that the government would do. The Minister was not going to decide about psychotherapy. That is still their position. In a letter to me dated 13 January 1993, the Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Tim Yeo, wrote, and I quote:

I was very interested to learn of the commendable progress that the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy has been making towards a unified umbrella organisation for psychotherapy. The forthcoming Register is of particular interest and a necessary step in progressing towards regulation. We will continue to watch closely the development of the Register over the next few years. Before official recognition can be considered we will need to be satisfied that it represents all the major psycho-therapeutic approaches.

We have managed to move from the hostility of 1978 to the mutuality of 1993 in a series of steps. Graham Bright MP introduced a Private Member's Bill to the House of Commons to regulate the practice of psychotherapy in 1981. It fell at second reading on a technicality, which is the fate of most Private Member's Bills. As nothing further seemed to be happening, and in order to use the momentum that had started, the British Association for Counselling invited as many organisations as possible to a symposium at their headquarters in Rugby to discuss the Foster and Sieghart Reports. Thus the Rugby Psychotherapy Conference was born in 1981. The Rugby Conference became the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy (UKSCP) in 1989 and then was renamed the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP) in 1993 in preparation for the launch of the Register.

On Touching a Patient

Viqui Rosenberg

Viqui Rosenberg

6 Ridge Road, London N8 9LG

Viqui Rosenberg  

This paper explores the conflicting as well as complementary relation between interpretation and touch in psychotherapy. It attempts to make sense of a clinical experience in which the change of orientation and framework undergone by the therapist in the course of a patient's treatment provided an opportunity for the therapeutic relationship to move from a body-therapy approach to a psychoanalytic one. It suggests that this particular experience may offer opportunities for discussing some problems encountered in the field of clinical practice.

The Universality of Shame: A Psychoanalytic Approach

Malcolm Pines

Malcolm Pines

88 Montagu Mansions, London W1H 1LF

Malcolm Pines  

In this paper shame is viewed from several different perspectives: culturally, socially and developmentally. As an emotion shame is shaped by culture and serves as a boundary for the protection of privacy; developmentally shame engenders the awareness of the self and its vulnerabilities. Recognition of shame proneness and defences against it can enhance the therapist's sensitivity and warn against the insensitivity and omnipotence that can often develop unwittingly.

1: Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

Anthony Ryle

CAT Office, Munro Clinic
Guy's Hospital
London SE1

Anthony Ryle  

It's a slightly tall order to discuss mind and self in half an hour; I may not try to cover the question. What I will try to do is to outline my view of the similarities and differences between the two models, with a particular emphasis on theory rather than practice. To do that I shall have to assume some familiarity on your part with CAT.

In a general way CAT is both centrally derived from psychoanalysis, and has been busy differentiating itself in certain ways, and in some ways stands in a critical stance towards it. There are clear common features, in so far as in both the understanding of the developmental origins of personality and relationship patterns is central; the common formation of personality and interpersonal factors in relation to others is agreed; and the recognition and use of transference play a central part in the treatment in both models.

The main differences, I think, are the higher level of activity for both patients and therapists in CAT, and the emphasis on patient participation; the use of descriptive reformulation rather than interpretation for reasons which I will come back to; the extensive use of written materials in the therapy; and quite a lot of differences in the way the theory of development and of therapeutic influence is understood. It's those differences which I'm going to primarily try and address.

But just to give you the headlines, for those who aren't familiar. As its name suggests it's an integrative model, drawing primarily on cognitive psychology, cognitive therapy and psychoanalysis. Its key distinguishing feature is the practice of the reformulation of the patient's problems very early in the therapy, usually by the fourth session. Based upon the history, the early interaction in the room, the patient's self-monitoring, and the patient's reading, the therapist is required to produce a letter addressed to the patient, which is in draft and which is agreed with the patient. Essentially it is a re-narration of the patient's story, attempting to put more emphasis (where it's missing) on meanings and feelings attached to events and to clarify what the patient was and was not responsible for. It's a strange moment, reading the letter: although we're giving back the patient their own story, it's often profoundly moving, and is certainly a very important bonding in the therapeutic task.

[[RunningHead]]

Of Sentiments and Sensations

Luis Sierra

Luis Sierra

63 Lancaster Road, London W11 1QG

Luis Sierra  

In psychoanalytic thinking the affect theory presents special difficulties. The affect has been described as the qualitative expression of the quantity of instinctual energy and of its fluctuations.

Rapaport pointed out that we do not possess a systematic statement of the theory of affect and that many of the concepts encountered by the student of psychoanalytic theory are often imprecise and sometimes contradictory. According to Rapaport (1953), the theory of affects integrates three components: inborn affect, dischargechannels and discharge-threshold of drive cathexis; the use of these inborn channels as safety valves and indicators of drive tension, the modification of their threshholds by drives and derivative motivations, prevented from drive-action and the formation thereby of the drive-representation turned affect-chart; and the progressive ‘taming’ and advancing ego control, in the course of psychic structure-formation, of the affects which are thereby turned into affect-signals released by the ego.

One common but potent source of confusion is that of identifying the theory of anxiety with the theory of affects in general. The latter includes the former but is not identical to it. The special nature of anxiety and its differences from other affects is something I will mention only, as expanding on it is beyond the scope of this essay. I would like to mention here Anna Freud's (1936) The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence since it distinguishes between those defences which are directed against anxiety and those which are employed against other affective states. The distinction between the role of anxiety and measures to avoid other kinds of psychic pain is crucial.

The way in which different groups of people deal with their feelings is what concerns us today and for my presentation I have selected individuals who, among the many different ways of attempting to deal with painful feelings, often replace them with the sensations provoked by virtue of pharmacological intoxication.

Competencies: Reservations, Risks and Developments - A Response to Chris Whyte

Richard Morgan-Jones

Richard Morgan-Jones

25 Lewes Road, Eastbourne, BN21 2BY

Richard Morgan-Jones  

I write in response to the ‘Personal View’ published in the British Journal of Psychotherapy by Chris Whyte (1994). He writes of his fears about the current attempts by the UKCP to develop a competency-based assessment to qualify psychotherapists under the Government's National Vocational Qualifications scheme. I write to support his reservations and to add to his views in order to begin to explore some of the complexities of the current political/professional situation. I then want to explore some of the risks involved and to propose some first thoughts on what competencies in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy already look like, as I believe they can be seen in current training practice, if often unarticulated.

Crossing the Threshold

Gail Yariv

Gail Yariv

121 York Road, Montpelier, BS6 5QG

Gail Yariv  

The very first moments of contact with a patient may provide a vital clue to the core dynamic of the therapeutic process.

Some analysts have stressed the importance of the first dream of an analysis. Others have focused on the first session as being seminal. In this paper I want to raise a few questions about what goes on in the very first moments of meeting a patient and its potential implications for the subsequent work. I shall try to differentiate the nature of what occurs and suggest that such differentiations might contribute to assessment, particularly where the initial interview is also the first session with the same therapist.

Psychoanalysis and Feminism

Margot Waddell

Margot Waddell

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Margot Waddell  

Juliet Mitchell's presentation put me in mind of some lines of Yeats's which I often find myself quoting:

God guard me from those thoughts

Men think in the mind alone.

He that sings a lasting song

Thinks in a marrow bone.

(W.B. Yeats A Prayer of Old Age)

As most here will know, the publication of Psychoanalysis and Feminism in 1974 marked a historically significant coming together of a number of forces, economically, politically, and culturally specific and interrelated in extremely complex ways. In this country, the forces arose essentially from the politicization of the younger generation in the sixties during which protests against American imperialism re-awakened hopes of change for all oppressed people and a commitment to try to bring that about - to do something about things.

The publication also stimulated a desire to think about things: it initiated a debate which has been dramatically growing in strength and depth ever since. As Juliet Mitchell says, in important respects the book arose from a lack - an absence in the largely male-dominated discourse of Marxism of an analysis of the internal world as well as of the external. Many of us belonged to Marx/Freud reading groups at the time - grappling with the kinds of issues she describes and moving towards a position that psychoanalysis, far from being the enemy of the woman's movement was, in fact, essential to it.

This position was brilliantly articulated in the pages of Juliet Mitchell's book. The rich harvest of that extraordinarily important statement has been reaped during these 20 years, most significantly by promoting thought in these matters, whether in agreement or in opposition to Juliet Mitchell's way of seeing things - thought which then provoked action.

Politically the situation has, of course, completely changed since then. There has been a collapse of the left as we knew it. Many, I think, have turned to psychoanalysis not only as a refuge for their damaged selves, but also to seek enlightenment about the irrational, intransigent and destructive aspects of us all, which forever variously undermine efforts to move on, compel to repeat, or propel towards accommodation to the status quo.

In Praise of Once-Weekly Work: Making a Virtue of Necessity or Treatment of Choice?

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NW1 8YD

Gertrud Mander  

This paper attempts to evaluate the once-weekly psychodynamic model and to outline the therapeutic principles and methodology on which it is based. Using Freud's concept of ‘psychotherapy for the people’, issues of time, frame, technique, and transference are discussed in relation to this model which draws on and adapts psychoanalytic theory and technique to suit its less intensive, but equally long-term practice. Some fundamental questions are raised in relation to higher frequencies of attendance, the status attached to numbers, the use of theory, choice of and suitability for once-weekly work.

Psychotherapy Grounded in the Feminine Principle by Barbara Stevens Sullivan. Published by Chiron Publications, Wilmette, Illinois, 1992; 205 pages; £13.99.

Val Richards

Val Richards

London

Val Richards  

The mission of this book is to reclaim what the author holds to be the underrepresented and repressed feminine principle in psychotherapy. Stressing that the ‘feminine’ is in no way confined to women, but is an essential feature of both sexes, and careful to proclaim the equal importance of the masculine factor, she appeals for a more balanced dialectic between the two. Both male and female are ‘energic patterns of being’, present in all people at all times, archetypes to be constellated in both sexes and functioning as two opposed metaphors. Because this review will attend primarily to Sullivan's application of the feminine principle, it is essential to acknowledge her appreciation of the masculine, expressed especially in the chapter entitled ‘The Role of the Masculine’, and her affirmation of the value of the analytic frame.

While Sullivan's conceptualisation of the feminine is part of an upsurge in Jungian analytic theory, notably in the United States, (and evident, for example, in The Plural Psyche (Samuels 1989)), the particular slant, indeed the distinction, here, is Sullivan's alignment of the feminine principle with Jungian and Object Relations approaches to theory and practice. She refers primarily to Winnicott, whose ‘orientation comes from a feminine centre’, contrasting this with the drive theory of Freud, and perhaps it is not surprising that what we have taken to be the essential characteristics of Object Relations and of Jungian theory, without gender bias, turn out to be saluted by Sullivan as epitomising the feminine. Stating that ‘this book is about the holding - the nursing - that occupies the majority of time in any therapeutic venture’, she may appear at first to disregard the ingredients of challenge and rigour, but this is stoutly countered by feisty material from her own practice.

Sullivan's most creative and illuminating contributions from a feminine perspective revolve around the following: comparative concepts of the self in relation to the function of myth and archetypes; the advocacy of regression to the depths of the psyche with a positive approval of ‘merger’ (i.e. fusion, primary unity) and loss of boundaries; the privileging of ‘not knowing’, which is ‘feminine’, above diagnosis, labelling and interpretation, which count as ‘masculine’.

Psychic Retreats by John Steiner. Published by Routledge, London, 1993; 162 pages; £ 12.99 (paperback).

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto

LCP, London

Jane Kitto  

This book is subtitled Pathological Organizations in Psychotic, Neurotic and Borderline Patients. The author tells us at the start that his concern is primarily clinical: ‘My central preoccupation is the way organizations function in individual patients in individual sessions during an analysis’. This is the strength of the book.

What Steiner calls the pathological organisation has a long history which he traces back to Freud, Abraham, and more recent writers such as Joan Riviere, Rosenfeld, Segal and Joseph. He argues that such an organisation is connected with primitive destructiveness and cites Freud's remark that there can be obstacles to change running so deep that we have to assume the operation of the death instinct (1937). Violence or neglect in the environment may result in the internalisation of violent disturbed objects which in turn become ‘receptacles for the projection of the individual's own destructiveness’. Steiner draws on the work of Klein and others, including Bion's ideas on violent splitting and projection.

The emphasis is on organisation, as in Rosenfeld's dramatic description, in his paper of 1971, of the mafia gang. Following Klein (1935), Steiner proposes that the organisation is experienced by the patient as a retreat, a relatively anxiety-free state, situated between the paranoid schizoid and the depressive positions, a kind of siding or layby. The technical problems facing the analyst are, first, the stuckness of the situation and, second, the lure of the organisation, where peace from anxiety and guilt is bought at the price of complicity, so that the analyst has to ‘struggle with his own propensity both to fit in and collude with the organisation on the one hand, and to withdraw into his own defensive retreat on the other’. The book is full of examples of sequences from sessions illustrating these difficulties, and Steiner is refreshingly frank about mistakes and failures.

Boredom in the Therapist: Countertransference Issues

Jean Flannery

Jean Flannery

8 Church Drive
Lincoln LN6 7AX

Jean Flannery  

When a therapist is bored in the clinical session this is always, unless pathological, a countertransference issue. Understanding the causes and meanings of this boredom thus adds to an understanding of the therapeutic process and relationship. It may have a variety of causal factors which need teasing out in the furtherance of the therapeutic process. Boredom may be connected with feelings of emptiness or drowsiness but is in itself a distinct phenomenon.

R.D. Laing: A Biography by Adrian Charles Laing. Published by Peter Owen, London and Chester Springs, PA 1994; 248 pages; £25.00.

James Hood

James Hood

London

James Hood  

R.D. Laing, although granted the rituals accorded to an honoured son of Scotland, where he still has mythical status - portrait in the National Gallery, Edinburgh, funeral service and burial at Glasgow Cathedral - with his reputation already tarnished by his terminal decline, disappeared from public view until the publication of this book. Headline writers then took him up with a vengeance: ‘Doomed guru of the divided self’ Financial Times); ‘Psychiatrist, heal thyself (Glasgow Herald); ‘Drunk in charge’ (Times Literary Supplement). ‘Ronnie’ Laing made the headlines in the mid-to late-sixties; his rise to fame was meteoric - but so was his fall from grace.

Adrian Laing, the second of R.D. Laing's six sons, a lawyer, not a therapist, told his father before he died in 1989 that he intended to write this account; the book obsessed him for four years prior to its publication; he consulted and interviewed widely and had access to very extensive archives. Illuminated by personal anecdotes, which can offer comic relief from sometimes painful content, it is not a memoir but an official biography, an authentic account of the one British psychiatrist of the past 40 years who became a prominent star in the North Atlantic firmament.

The author carefully plots Laing's course from modest lower-middle-class family, extraordinarily gifted musically and medically, apprenticeships in Glasgow and the R.A.M. C., Tavistock-based research, authorship and public lectures, to the creative ferment and group work which formed the base from which he launched himself into fame. The Divided Self, still in the view of some his greatest book, was by contrast the result of a solo effort in Laing's mid to late twenties, solo with this proviso: before publication he had passed the manuscript around the senior colleagues who constituted until then the ‘containing environment’ of his ‘Tavi’ and psychoanalytic training institutes. These included Sutherland, Bowlby, Winnicott, Marion Milner and Charles Rycroft. How Laing, always a recalcitrant student, was accepted and eventually passed out as a qualified psychoanalyst is recounted in fascinating and amusing detail.

Emotion and Unconscious Phantasy: Chairman's Remarks on the Papers by Andre Green and Rosine Jozef Perelberg

David Bell

David Bell

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

David Bell  

The title of our conference today is, I think, deliberately ambiguous: it refers to both a conceptual problem, namely, ‘how do we theorize affect’ and to a clinical issue ‘how do we learn to experience our feelings, without disowning them or being overwhelmed by them, and thus become able to think about them’. Green's paper concerns the former and Perelberg's the latter. In this discussion of these two papers I will first make some comments that derive from a philosophical perspective and then discuss the two papers in turn. In concluding I will suggest that some of the theoretical difficulties raised by Green can be overcome by utilizing the approach developed by Bion, to some extent, Perelberg's paper demonstrates.

Freud's discoveries have had great import for the philosophy of mind and, reciprocally, work arising from within the philosophy of mind has, I believe, great relevance for psychoanalytic theories - not for deciding between theories, or justifying a particular theory, but for understanding what is logically, as opposed to psychologically, entailed by holding a particular theory.

Feelings are clearly not the same thing as emotions and, although it might seem plausible to identify emotion with feeling or feeling states, it is clearly not the case that this works in reverse. There are many feelings which are clearly not emotions - such as the feeling that ‘I got it wrong’, or that ‘that is John’, or ‘that isn't by Mozart’. These are examples of feeling states that may have emotional consequences but they are not emotions. There is something in the nature of what it is to have a feeling that pushes us towards thinking of it as an event experienced in consciousness (in the descriptive sense) whereas this is not true for emotions. Richard Wollheim (1992) takes the view that emotions are dispositions. They form a background to our phenomenal world influencing it, yet beyond awareness. They are part of our attitude; they colour or flavour our perceptions. They are not beliefs nor desires, though they have an intrinsic relation to belief and desire. This attitudinal quality of emotions corresponds, I think, to Green's ‘tonality’. Emotions can be mental states or, as Wollheim puts it, emotional dispositions manifest themselves in mental states. Dispositions have close connections both to belief and desire.

This book is in turn engaging, reassuring and provocative. Richards uses psychoanalysis - primarily Kleinian in orientation - to analyse the pleasures and constraints of engagement with various aspects of popular leisure pursuits. These include watching football, visiting the country, driving, cigarette smoking and listening to pop music. He bases his critique on a particular ‘psychoanalytic sensibility’, based on interpretations of associations and awareness of his own position within popular culture.

Richards argues that popular culture offers the opportunity for the expression and gratification of primitive libidinal satisfactions within secure and authoritative, collectively sanctioned boundaries. In Winnicottian terms, popular culture provides a series of contained spaces for play. Richards argues that this facilitates both the working through of personal developmental difficulties and offers a means of expression within the wider social community.

Richards illustrates his thesis with a number of closely argued concrete accounts. He shows, for example, in a detailed analysis of song lyrics and personal biographies of pop stars, how pop music may offer the adolescent (or adult, for that matter) the opportunity to work through issues of separation and loss, to manage hostile and ambivalent feelings and to come to terms with his or her developing sexuality. Another rich chapter examines the way in which football provides a vehicle for libidinal pleasures and the opportunity to re-enact adjustment to difficult social constraints. The Unconscious at Work: Individual and Organizational Stress in the Human Services edited by Anton Obholzer and Vega Zagier Roberts. Published by Routledge, London, 1994; 224 pages.

Deborah Marks

Deborah Marks

University of Sheffield

Deborah Marks  

This impressive volume offers a series of short, accessible accounts of work carried out by members of the Tavistock Clinic Consulting to Institutions Workshop. Unlike most edited collections, the book reads like a truly collective enterprise. The sense of shared goals and analytic approaches owes much to the shared institutional background of the authors. The chapters are skilfully woven together by the linking work of the editors.

Rooted in Kleinian and systems theory and following the ground-breaking work of Menzies Lyth, Trist, Jaques and Rice, the central proposition of the book is that institutions are not governed by conscious and purely rational ways of organising. The authors describe anxieties generated by work in the human services and the attendant social relationships which may be managed by instituting a series of defence mechanisms which serve to keep psychic pain and conflict at bay. These defences are unconscious, to the extent that they appear as taken for granted and unquestionable aspects of institutional practices. The effect of these defences may be to undermine the capacity of the institution to deal with the pragmatic realities of work.

Part one of the book offers an exceptionally clear introductory exposition of the contribution from psychoanalysis (primarily Kleinian in orientation), the work of Bion and a review of the contribution from open systems theory.

further. Looking around this hall I find myself wondering about the almost palpable atmosphere of high anticipation. What has brought 400 people together today? Which internal chords have resonated to the Freud Museum call and how has a distant storm in women's self-awareness contributed to this ground-swell 20 years on?

Like most audiences we have come here today to listen, learn, share our ideas. Hopefully people will feel free to speak openly despite the large numbers. Yet, on reflection, it seems to me that we have also gathered here with another purpose - not only to remember the past, nor even to take stock of the many material and conceptual changes that have occurred over the two decades since the ground-breaking publication of Psychoanalysis and Feminism. We have come to celebrate our achievements but in addition, in the spirit of both the women's movement and psychoanalytic itself, I believe we may have also chosen to come back 20 years after that formative period to re-evaluate ourselves from within. For this reason, I shall introduce a personal note and speak here of events in my life I have not until now voiced in public.

If in many ways, and to each in our own way, today might be regarded as a day of reckoning one of the main questions we must ask is - what in our own subjective psychohistories has brought each of us to seek that intricate combination of psychoanalysis and feminism in our lives, and how, in our daily lives, can we utilize the one to extend our understanding of the other? Speaking for myself, I feel a great many aspects of my own life converge at this point in time - both in terms of momentous political events and, on a smaller scale, a revival and integration of many old and complex interconnections with the past (represented by participants here and even connections with this building, from my training in town planning in a ‘previous life’).

[[RunningHead]]

Introduction to the Conference: Hysteria - 100 Years Since Freud

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

117 Borough High Street, London SE1 1NP

Jean Arundale  

The British Journal of Psychotherapy, Vol. 9(2) published a special section entitled ‘100 Years of Psychoanalysis’ which consisted of a group of papers that examined and re-evaluated Freud's concept of hysteria. The publication of these papers was received with interest and formed the basis of a conference held conjointly by the BJP and the Freud Museum in February 1994. Bob Hinshelwood, the founder/editor of the British Journal of Psychotherapy set the framework for these papers by writing in his editorial introduction that psychoanalysis is the only nineteenth-century treatment within psychiatry that has survived into the end of this century and is thus the oldest treatment in psychiatry. As such, it is ripe for removal unless it speaks in some specially apt way to the condition of man today. In this context, we will be looking at hysteria as a cultural entity, at its history, its role in the development of psychoanalytic theory, and what seem to be its new permutations found in the consulting-room.

The defining characteristic of hysteria in the nineteenth century was the conversion symptom. Women suffered from mysterious paralyses of parts of the body, convulsions and faints. There were strange disturbances of sensation, blindness, deafness and anaesthesias in some obscure leap from the mind to the body. David Smith's paper tracks the development of Freud's thoughts on the question of how the mind and body are related. From a ‘split consciousness’ theory and the philosophical background of Cartesian dualism with which hysteria was associated, Freud moved to a unitary theory, of the identity of the mind and brain which provided the philosophical underpinnings of his theory of the unconscious and aligns him with the majority of philosophers today. In his endeavour to understand how these otherwise intelligent women succumbed to the irrationality of a body dysfunction without neurological explanation, Freud's contribution was to alter the notion that it was ‘innate mental feebleness’, nervous degeneracy, or attention seeking that underlay the symptoms, but rather an illness of psychological origin. Freud made it known that the mental weakness was a result of the splitting of the psyche and not the other way around, a cause of the illness. And memories were the motive for splitting, or dissociation as it was then called. Ann Scott's paper looks at the way in which ‘hysterics suffer from reminiscences’, indicating the fate of repressed sexuality, how memories are retained and displaced, relocated in some sense in the body of the hysteric and not evacuated as in other disorders.

responseSet.title: Is There Any Logic in Feelings? An Introduction to Matte Blanco's Theory of Emotions
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Is There Any Logic in Feelings? An Introduction to Matte Blanco's Theory of Emotions

Eric Rayner PHD

Eric Rayner

43 Heath Hurst Road, London NW3 2RU

Eric Rayner  

Most people do not know much about Matte Blanco's bi-logic, so I will first present something about his fundamental conceptions and afterwards work towards a finale about feelings. These basic conceptions turn out to be extremely simple but they are so general, so abstract, that they are maddening to grasp. With this warning, off we go.

Freud's greatest contribution was, perhaps, to show that certain fundamental forms of transformation, representation or symbolization were taking place in the mind: a conscious idea or act could stand for some other experience but the link between the two was often not apparent. Unconscious processes were inferred as taking place. Freud showed that these unconscious processes do not obey the ordinary rules of logic. In fact he spelt out especially five characteristics of the unconscious which highlighted the differences from conscious level thought. These were displacement, condensation, timelessness, absence of mutual contradiction and replacement of external by internal reality.

These characteristics provided a start for Matte-Blanco. He was fascinated by Freud's systematic definition of such mental operations for the first time in history. But they are a disparate list. Surely, Matte thought, as unconscious processes can, at least sometimes, be understandable, they cannot be random; so they must obey some underlying rule or rules. If these fundamentals could be found then how much easier analytic work could be (Matte Blanco 1975, 1988; see also Rayner 1995).

Here Matte started at a different conceptual position from Freud but he still saw his ideas as complementing not contradicting classical analysis. Matte's stress was upon ways of knowing or cognitive structures, his interest is epistemological. As well as - not instead of - psychodynamics, analysis must also be about knowledge with its implications, negations, contradictions, paradoxes, confusions, distortions and obliteration. Logic and illogic are central to analysis.

One or two concepts new to analysis are central; the first is that of a set. Animals and especially we humans proceed through the world by discriminating the things around us and recognizing the many different relationships between them - here memory is vital. All the time we are discriminating differences and registering samenesses. Next, one of the functions of thinking is the conscious or unconscious ordering of this data into collections. This is essential as part of any act of recognition. An idea which recalls something else involves registration of at least one characteristic in common between the ideas. Such a characteristic acts to define the mental collection, set or class of all the things which possess that characteristic. In mathematics, the term ‘set’ is used to specify any collection of data: elements, objects or individuals.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Summary: Affects versus Representations or Affects as Representations?

Andre Green

Andre Green

Andre Green  

It is customary to begin this topic by saying that there is no present satisfactory theory of affects although a hundred or more theories exist. Rather than trying to build up a realistic portrait or likeness of particular affects, I prefer to use conceptual tools to create a representation of affect as a psychical construct.

Psychoanalytic theory is two-fold: it is a theory of psychoanalytic practice and a general theory of psychical activity, and each must be in close connection with the other. But many of the challenging new theories do not obey this requirement. New clinical and theoretical concepts, often borrowed from neighbouring fields, are contradictory, making it difficult to decide which theory is good and which has to be rejected. It has been said that Freud's metapsychology itself has to be abandoned but I do not recommend this. But whether one agrees with Freud or not, a psychoanalytic theory of affects must take a stand on the existence of unconscious affects and their relationship with conscious affects and other components of mental life.

The Observation of Affects

Although there is a general consensus that affects are rooted in the very beginnings of mental life, a developmental approach is not really helpful in solving the difficulties. To explain: (1) Infant observation is unable to give us an idea of what goes on in the psychic processes of the adult internal world, especially in the unconscious. (2) Infant research has value for understanding the infant but is less significant in the elaboration of psychoanalytic theory. The proposed changes based on infant research would transform psychoanalytic theory in a direction that moves away from the basic principles of psychoanalysis. It draws data from a source not compatible with the two-fold areas of clinical practice and theoretical development. (3) Many of the so-called new theories born of infant observation such as self-relatedness or intersubjectivity already exist in psychoanalytic theory, initially stated in a different way by Lacan, Mahler, Winnicott, Kohut and others. Philosophers have attempted to deal with the complex matter of affects, seeing them as internalized structures leading to action.

[[RunningHead]]

Female Perversion and Hysteria

Estela Welldon

Estela Welldon

8 Fitzjohn's Avenue, London NW3

Estela Welldon  

This paper was prompted by Freud's axiom that hysteria was the negative of perversion. I claimed ignorance on the subject but felt challenged by the possibilities in the light of change since Freud's time, when hysteria was the female counterpart of male perversion. Tied in with my own clinical findings was Juliet Mitchell's concern with male hysteria; we started to sketch out some comparisons with a view to future work.

I would now like to offer my views on female perversion, our initial views on hysteria and perversion, and a clinical case to illustrate a few points.

Female Perversion

In my view, as I have written elsewhere (Welldon 1988), some of the psychodynamic principles operating in perversion appear in females when they become mothers. A woman's capacity for getting pregnant and containing the baby within her own body provides her with some of the same emotional characteristics in her objectrelationships as are found in exaggerated and highly distorted forms in perverse relationships. These include the desire and intention to engulf the other person, to dehumanise the object, to intrude into, to invade, to be in complete control of and to merge with the other.

Motherhood is sometimes chosen for unconscious perverse reasons. ‘The woman would know that in achieving motherhood she is automatically achieving the role of master, that of being in charge, in complete control of another being who has to submit himself or herself not only emotionally but also biologically to the mother's demands, however inappropriate they may be’ (Welldon 1988, p. 81).

Hysteria and Perversion

There is considerable overlap between perversion and hysteria, and therefore differentiating factors are important. The following are a few considerations that emerged during discussions between Juliet Mitchell and myself; we believe that they may be useful to aid the accuracy of diagnostic evaluations and during treatment. As is customary in dealing with dynamic issues we have found that some of the points account for a number of differences, some are equals, and some overlap. Whenever hysteria is mentioned in this paper the opinions are attributable to Mitchell, whereas when perversion is mentioned they are my own opinions unless other authors or names are used and mentioned.

[[RunningHead]]

‘Reclaimed Once More by the Realities of Life’: Hysteria and the Location of Memory

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

16a Glyn Mansions, Avonmore Road, London W14 8XH

Ann Scott  

Just as the first dream represented her turning away from the man she loved to her father - that is to say, her flight from life into disease - so the second dream announced that she was about to tear herself free from her father and had been reclaimed once more by the realities of life. (Freud 1905, p. 122)

The quotation that forms the first part of my title is taken from the closing words of Freud's ‘Dora’, poignant and aggressive on Freud's part as they have always struck me as being. I also find them deeply evocative, at the level of psychic life. How much does life claim us; how much are we claimed by our past, by memories of our past? My paper is organised around the paradoxical role that memory can play: it can make free - like life, be an agent for reclamation - while in its inaccessibility it can haunt. We seek ways of theorising both the remembered and the unremembered, and ways of thinking about what it is that memories are memories of. Here one possibility might be that memories that are able to be held within the psyche are of a different order of experience from those that are projected out, expelled. It is this theme - the location of memory - that I explore here, considering differences between ‘classical’ hysteria (in Freud's work) and ‘hysteria today’, the theme of this conference. I want to pose a group of questions: what happens to the memories - to use Freud's terms, the reminiscences - from which the hysteric suffers? Classically they are abreacted in speech. But if they are not abreacted, might they become located in another: a person, or, perhaps, a place that represents psychic space? Because we cannot separate our thinking from a more recent psychoanalytic and therapeutic language, it is clear that I'm hinting at wider questions - broadly, under the heading of splitting and projection - and at a larger number of disorders than the hysterias. But my focus today remains the hysterical as denoting questions about the body and its registration of the sexual: whether experienced or fantasied.

I need an airlift. Anybody? Any CAT therapists around? I need a reformulation. I had an earlier draft of Tony's paper and I have a terrible sense of the goalposts having been just slightly moved. I had a thought about leaving [Laughter], but then I thought: I give myself an interpretation instead. ‘The only thing is, stop thinking that he's your father. Don't worry about it.’ [Laughter]

Introduction

The psychoanalytic literature on the mind and the self is just about co-terminous with the entire psychoanalytic corpus. You will not be surprised that I too shall fight shy of summarising it in the next 30 minutes. Nor do I want to spend the time allocated to me by offering an unrequited psychoanalytic critique of CAT. I would be reluctant to do that, primarily because there is much that I greatly admire in Tony Ryle's work which I have followed fairly closely over the last 15 or so years and which he so clearly summarised for us this evening. I particularly respect the exceptional combination of a desire for theoretical purity and technical eclecticism which CAT represents. I share his conviction that psychotherapeutic technique should be pragmatically innovative and intellectually adventurous. I, along with the majority of outcome researchers, do not share his optimism concerning brief therapy, as I think the evidence from well controlled studies points to at best 20-25% long-term improvement following even the better structured psychotherapeutic intervention with chronic psychiatric patients (Roth & Fonagy, in press). However, a discussion on the efficacy of brief interventions would not go very far in addressing our ambitious topic for this evening. So what I have decided to do as a compromise is to identify a very selected set of psychoanalytic ideas which relate to the question of the mind and self, and try to integrate these with Tony Ryle's paper this evening to the best of my ability and knowledge.

The ‘Self versus Self-Representation

Confusion and ambiguity surround the status of the concept of self in psychoanalysis, particularly whether it is a theoretical (meta-psychological) construct of a system in the mind, part of our psychoanalytic theory of the mind, or an experiential one relating to the person's cumulative affective experience. The Truth about Freud's Technique: The Encounter with the Real by M. Guy Thompson. Published by New York University Press, 1994; 279 pages; £35.95.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

IPSS, London

Paul Gordon  

No article or book on psychoanalysis is complete, it seems, unless it carries its quota of references to Freud. There is nothing wrong with this in itself of course; we should be surprised if there were no acknowledgements at all to the man who first formulated the parameters of our ‘impossible profession’. And yet, too frequently, Freud is cited in the way that I was once taught to cite legal cases, as authority, as establishing the truth of a particular statement, almost without the need for further argument. In addressing the question of ‘the truth about Freud's technique’, Mike Thompson, an American psychoanalyst who worked at the Philadelphia Association in London with R.D. Laing and his colleagues, is not out to rubbish Freud. Rather he wants to reclaim Freud as the man who said that his whole concern throughout his life was the pursuit of truth, the man for whom there was only one indispensable ‘rule’ of psychoanalysis: in effect, ‘say what you must and don't hide it’. The truth about Freud's technique is, Thompson argues, essentially about truth itself: know your own mind and the truth will set you free.

Although Freud was dismissive of philosophy - he said it was of interest only to a small number of intellectuals and was scarcely intelligible to anyone else - Thompson argues that Freud's quest for truth was inevitably a philosophical one, even if he never conceptualised it in philosophical terms. His reflections on the nature of reality were philosophical queries, not scientific investigations as he might have liked to think, and as so many of his followers have since claimed, and yet his tendency to equate reality with what was externally valid compromised his search for truth. For a better articulated idea of truth Thompson suggests that we look to the philosopher Martin Heidegger for whom the question of truth ‘is his philosophy in its entirety’. For Heidegger, truth is not about a ‘correspondence’ to things, rather truth becomes known by revealing what is hidden. Its opposite, untruth, is the concealment of truth and is, Thompson claims, remarkably similar to Freud's conception of repression.

Diversity and Psychoanalysis

Joanna Ryan PHD

Joanna Ryan

44 Lordship Road, London N16 0QT

Joanna Ryan  

One of the pleasures, as opposed to the anxieties, of preparing for this conference, has been to reread Psychoanalysis and Feminism, and in doing so to reconnect with many of the issues of the early seventies. I think that the convening of this conference is testimony to the classic status of this book, and to all the work and thought that have flowed from it. Psychoanalysis and Feminism has been part of the framework within which many of us have pursued our very diverse feminist and psychoanalytic goals over the last 20 years. And this is so, even if our goals have been very different from those expressed in the book. I want to emphasize this rich diversity both in psychoanalysis and feminism, a diversity which is very much represented here today and, I hope, one which we can stay with. The diversity encompasses a whole range of clinical and theoretical positions and projects, yet it can still be brought under the same heading. This is, I think, evidence of how much there still is to discuss and how much, as feminists in the nineties, we still do desire and perhaps need to find ways of talking to each other.

One of the questions that has always been of issue, and remains so, is what kind of relationship do we envisage between psychoanalysis and feminism? What is the nature of the ‘and’ between these two terms? In Psychoanalysis and Feminism Juliet Mitchell argued strongly that feminism needed psychoanalysis; and she put this in terms, as she saw it then, of the relationship between political practice and theory, in which feminism constituted the practice, and psychoanalysis the theory. She raised the question of whether the relation between feminism and psychoanalysis was equivalent to that between class struggle and Marxism, whether the analysis of ideology that she saw psychoanalysis as providing could inform the struggle against women's oppression.

The notion of psychoanalysis as providing an analysis of patriarchal ideology and of cultural transmission has been a very influential one, perhaps more so in academic, than in clinical contexts, and much work has come of it. However this concept also has its negative side: I think it has circumscribed ensuing debates in quite constricting ways. In the act of rescuing psychoanalysis from earlier feminist criticisms, all critique of psychoanalysis got lost. Furthermore, many positive feminist contributions to psychoanalysis didn't affect the mainstream as much as they might have done. And this is something I imagine we might wish to talk about more today.

The Newborn in the Intensive Care Unit: A Neuropsychoanalytic Prevention Model by Romana Negri. Published by The Roland Harris Memorial Library, Clunie Press (Karnac Books), London, 1994; 260 pages; £18.95.

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

London

Maria Rhode  

This is an important book. The author, Dr Romana Negri, has worked for nearly 20 years as an Infant Neuropsychiatric Consultant in Bergamo. She studied infant observation under Esther Bick and Martha Harris, and has more recently undertaken infant observations of babies in utero by means of ultrasound scans. These observations were supervised by Donald Meltzer who has contributed a foreword to the present book; and she has supplemented them by infant observations of the babies after birth and by long-term follow-ups. Although these studies, like the work of Alessandra Piontelli, have revealed many fascinating consistencies of individual characteristics between the time before birth and after, these findings are not the main concern of this book, from which four principal areas of relevance emerge. Firstly, and most importantly, Romana Negri presents the reader with the emotional experience of the seriously pre-term new-born, in real and prolonged danger of death and subjected to painful and invasive life-saving procedures. It is the sort of experience that witnesses seek to defend themselves against by asserting that the baby's behaviour is simply a consequence of neurological immaturity, or by focusing on the necessary interventions and technology. Romana Negri undertook minutely detailed, regular observations of these babies. They became individual human beings for her, as they do for the reader. On another level, it could be shown that one hour a week of an observer's attention brought about definite improvements in the babies' vital signs, a finding that she presented at the conference on infant observation held at the Tavistock Clinic in 1993.

Secondly, Dr Negri made infant observation an essential component of the method she developed for working with parents and with medical and nursing staff. Her detailed exposition of this method takes up roughly a third of the book, and should prove extremely useful to workers in this country. Thirdly, she made a careful study of early signs of disturbance, which she was able to differentiate according to whether the outcome in the absence of intervention was likely to be childhood psychosis or the syndrome associated with minimal brain damage. She developed a technique for early intervention which was effective in the great majority of cases. Fourthly, she documents the interplay between emotional and organic factors that she was able to trace in these very early conditions. Readers in this country, particularly non-medical readers, will find her overview of paediatric neurological literature and her integration of it with psychoanalytic theory particularly helpful, especially since much of the work on neuropsychiatry or psychomotricite has been done in Italy, France and Spain and is not easily accessible in Britain.

Loss of the Loved Object: Tragic and Moral Motifs in Melanie Klein's Concept of the Depressive Position

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Meira Likierman  

This paper offers a reading of Melanie Klein's concept of the depressive position based on primary texts. A problematic area is uncovered, resulting from a contradictory tension amongst phenomena grouped under Klein's concept. Specifically, the author notes two motifs that run through her descriptions, which are metaphorically labelled in this paper as ‘tragic’ and ‘moral’. These are shown to negate each other in experiential terms, as the more primitive ‘tragic’ level implies irrevocable loss and hence catastrophic states, whereas the more mature ‘moral’ level derives strength from reparation. These two motifs create a dialectic tension that enriches Klein's concept.

[[RunningHead]]

Feelings and their Absence from the Analytic Setting

Rosine Perelberg PHD

Rosine Perelberg

35 Hodford Road, London NW 11 8NL

Rosine Perelberg  

Introduction

In this paper I would like to examine the connection between feeling, thinking and acting out as related to the issue of violence. I will present clinical material derived from the analysis of two patients. One, a young male adult, had presented severe violent behaviour prior to the beginning of his analysis. The second, a middle-aged woman, was close to violence against the analyst in the consulting-room. Through their analysis I came to understand that for these patients violence represented an attempt to find a refuge from feelings towards the analyst which they experienced as unbearable. These feelings were related to terrifying phantasies about the relationship with the analyst, an imago of an all-engulfing mother and a belief in the primal scene as an act of violence (see Perelberg 1995a). When they came to analysis both patients lacked an affective understanding of these phantasies which were repeatedly externalized in their relationships.

In the first section of the paper I will outline some points of reference in the psychoanalytic literature on affect. I will then present some of my own thoughts on the theme, derived both from the literature and from my understanding of some of my patients in analysis. I will then examine some clinical material relating to two specific patients in the light of these hypotheses.

Some Points of Reference in the Literature

Throughout his work Freud continuously discussed the relationship between affect and idea as components of human experience. In the first phase of his work, Freud's formulations were couched in energy terms. Affect was equated with energy and symptoms represented the need for the mind to rid itself of large quantities of such affective energy to restore its equilibrium (Sandler 1982). Affect was linked to discharge and thus the link between affective experience and the body was stressed. Freud did not distinguish between the psychic and the somatic and discussed mainly the negative affects, such as those that denote suffering, distress or anxiety (Stein 1991, p. 5).

[[RunningHead]]

Group Analysis, Transculturality and Ethics

Dennis Brown

Dennis Brown

88 Montagu Mansions, London W1H 1LF

Dennis Brown  

The foundation matrix described by Foulkes embodies values, standards and myths of each culture as well as our common biological characteristics. The workshops of the European Association for Transcultural Group Analysis have revealed how much of this matrix is unconscious, taken for granted, until we are confronted by people of another culture or have to move from one culture to another. Such a move is often traumatic. The abuse of difference is integral to historical tragedy and trauma, but a move from paranoid destructiveness to depressive reparation is possible in favourable circumstances.
